power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

One of the most fundamental tensions in empirical social science is the gap between the observational data researchers collect and the causal claims they make out of it.
Plato already stipulated that " [e]verything that becomes or changes must do so owing to some cause; for nothing can come to be without a cause" (cited in Plato, 2000, p. 13).
text.formatted: Plato already stipulated that " <ref type="bibr">[e]</ref>verything that becomes or changes must do so owing to some cause; for nothing can come to be without a cause" (cited in Plato, 2000, p. 13).

text.text: As humans are apparently bound to think in terms of causality, considering why things happen is an essential part of the human nature (Asendorpf, 2012, p. 391; Kaltenpoth, 2024, p. 1). Pearl et al. (2016, p. xii) put the problem technically: "the fundamental question at the core of a great deal of statistical inference is causal; do changes in one variable cause changes in another, and if so, how much change do they cause?".

(2016, p. xii)</ref> put the problem technically: "the fundamental question at the core of a great deal of statistical inference is causal; do changes in one variable cause changes in another, and if so, how much change do they cause?".

text.text: Yet the traditional language of statistics offers no direct route to answering such questions.
Its tools were designed, as Ronald Fisher (1922, p. 311) already declared, for "the reduction of data", not for recovering the inference process that generated them.

text.text: The issue at hand is exacerbated for " [a]nalysts seek causation, but the data, on their own, only communicate associations" (Elwert, 2013, p. 247).

text.text: To overcome this constraint, experimental designs have been established as the current 'gold standard'.

The conventional methodological solution of randomized experimental designs, however, often falls short due to physical (i.e., real-life constraints which cannot be modeled experimentally), economic, ethical or other constraints (Levy, 2023, p. iii; Pearl et al., 2016, p. xi; Rohrer, 2018, p. 27).

text.text: Faced with these limitations, researchers heavily rely on observational data paired with statistical control of third variables as a "cornerstone of developing causal models" (Levy, 2023, p. 3).

text.text: More precisely, regressing dependent variables (i.e., outcomes) on independent variables (i.e., exposures) while conditioning on (i.e., controlling for) measured covariates thought to account for potential confounding.
In this context, the choice of control variables in practice "is determined by norms in the domain and by the variables available in the data set" (Rohrer, 2018, p. 28).

text.text: In this highly sensitive field of observational data, the effects of methodological biases are central for they potentially lead to systematic errors that abide with increasing sample sizes (Cole et al., 2010, p. 417).

text.text: According to Oeberst & Imhoff (2023, p. 4), the key findings from years of psychological research show that fundamentally biased information processing is "not only ubiquitous [...] but also a conditio humana" (see e.g., Abelson et al., 1968; Feldman, 1966; Gawronski & Strack, 2012; Nickerson, 1998).

text.text: Based on this observation, collider bias plays a crucial role for it "seems less intuitive" (Rohrer, 2018, p. 35) and is generally "difficult to grasp" (Pearl et al., 2016, p. 41).

text.text: To put it simply, collider bias occurs if an analysis is conditioning on a variable that is a common effect of two or more causally preceding variables (Elwert & Winship, 2014, p. 31; Pearl et al., 2016, p. 39; Rohrer, 2018, p. 34).
text.formatted: To put it simply, collider bias occurs if an analysis is conditioning on a variable that is a common effect of two or more causally preceding variables <ref type="bibr">(Elwert & Winship, 2014, p. 31;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al., 2016, p. 39;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rohrer, 2018, p. 34)</ref>.

text.text: It is especially consequential when it operates undetected within an established research design.
As its effects emerge systematically rather than randomly, genuine signal becomes indistinguishable from 'noise' without an explicit causal framework.

In the absence of such a framework, researchers face a fundamental challenge in drawing valid causal inferences from observational data without making assumptions explicit (Wysocki et al., 2022, p. 2).
text.formatted: In the absence of such a framework, researchers face a fundamental challenge in drawing valid causal inferences from observational data without making assumptions explicit <ref type="bibr">(Wysocki et al., 2022, p. 2)</ref>.

text.text: The present thesis examines this methodological problem in a specific and consequential empirical domain: the psychology of ideal partner preferences.
As introduced by Eastwick & Neff (2012, p. 667) most individuals are able to readily describe the qualities they would like in an ideal romantic partner.
text.formatted: As introduced by <ref type="bibr">Eastwick & Neff (2012, p. 667)</ref> most individuals are able to readily describe the qualities they would like in an ideal romantic partner.

text.text: These descriptions often vary considerably, with some people valuing a caring and supportive partner who provides affection during difficult times, while others place greater importance on traits such as confidence and social competence.
Whether these individually stated preferences predict whom people end up with, and how positively they evaluate them, is the central question of the partner preference-matching literature.
The preference-matching hypothesis states that people evaluate romantic partners more favorably the more closely a partner's attributes match their stated ideals (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5).
text.formatted: The preference-matching hypothesis states that people evaluate romantic partners more favorably the more closely a partner's attributes match their stated ideals <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5)</ref>.

text.text: If one rates intelligence as highly desirable, is one more likely to evaluate an intelligent partner positively?
Does this variation in preferences explain why people are romantically drawn to some individuals rather than others?

These questions are central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model (Fletcher et al., 1999 (Fletcher et al., , 2000;; Simpson et al., 2001) that have motivated decades of empirical investigation (Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485).
text.formatted: These questions are central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fletcher et al., 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fletcher et al., , 2000;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Simpson et al., 2001)</ref> that have motivated decades of empirical investigation <ref type="bibr">(Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this longevity, empirical support for the matching hypothesis has remained surprisingly inconsistent, and concerns about the causal validity of the underlying research designs have been largely unaddressed (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5; Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1).
text.formatted: Despite this longevity, empirical support for the matching hypothesis has remained surprisingly inconsistent, and concerns about the causal validity of the underlying research designs have been largely unaddressed <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: Against this backdrop, Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 5) conducted the most comprehensive investigation of ideal partner preference-matching to date.
text.formatted: Against this backdrop, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 5)</ref> conducted the most comprehensive investigation of ideal partner preference-matching to date.

text.text: Partnering with the Psychological Science Accelerator (PSA), they collected data from N = 10,358 participants across 43 countries and 22 languages, systematically evaluated four distinct analytic approaches to measuring preference-matching, and concluded that idiosyncratic matching effects exist but are modest in size and highly dependent on how they are measured.

Their effort is laudable in many respects: the project was implemented as a preregistered report, draws on a sample of unparalleled scale and cross-cultural breadth, and makes the full dataset publicly available.
The latter provided the condition without which the present re-analysis would not have been possible.
At the same time, the impressive amount of data cannot resolve a structural shortcoming that is built into the sampling design itself.
The primary analysis which is dedicated to considering the matching hypothesis utilized a sample of established couples and singles rating their (most desired) partner.
As indicated earlier and described in much more detail in the theoretical framework, this configuration reflects conditioning on a collider variable.
Stated ideal preferences and perceived partner attributes both influence romantic evaluation, which in turn determines relationship formation as a common effect.
Romantic evaluation and the relationship status are therefore colliders inducing corresponding collider bias.
Conditioning on them, as every study using (most desired) partners necessarily does, opens potentially spurious paths between ideals and partner attributes before any analysis begins.
In other words, the analysis presupposes a selection event which represents a world where high romantic evaluation is given by construction.
An impressively large sample conditioned on a collider variable does not yield less biased estimates; it yields the same structural bias with greater precision.
That may even lead readers to endorse the wrong conclusions more confidently.

The present thesis operationalizes this critique by addressing the following research question: "To what extent does collider bias distort the predictive validity of ideal partner preferences in the Eastwick et al. (2024) data analysis?".
text.formatted: The present thesis operationalizes this critique by addressing the following research question: "To what extent does collider bias distort the predictive validity of ideal partner preferences in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> data analysis?".

text.text: To approach this question, the primary regression analyses of Eastwick et al. (2024) are replicated as a validated benchmark.
text.formatted: To approach this question, the primary regression analyses of <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> are replicated as a validated benchmark.

text.text: Subsequently, a hierarchical multivariate extension is developed to analytically consider the collider bias configuration.
Finally, both results are compared and assessed regarding potential predictive validity and valid causal inference.
The overall aim of this thesis is thus to develop an analytically rigorous approach to deal with the partner preferencematching hypothesis.

The evaluation of the analysis conducted by Eastwick et al. (2024) revealed several additional sources of bias which primarily need to be addressed to properly account for collider bias in a subsequent analysis.
text.formatted: The evaluation of the analysis conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> revealed several additional sources of bias which primarily need to be addressed to properly account for collider bias in a subsequent analysis.

text.text: Based on this observation, four hypotheses guide the empirical analysis.

The theoretical baseline, formally H0, restates Eastwick et al.'s (2024, p. 5) preference-matching hypothesis as described above, predicting positive and significant interaction effects between partner and ideal trait ratings across all 35 attributes for the original regression analysis.
text.formatted: The theoretical baseline, formally H0, restates <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al.'s (2024, p. 5)</ref> preference-matching hypothesis as described above, predicting positive and significant interaction effects between partner and ideal trait ratings across all 35 attributes for the original regression analysis.

text.text: As Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48) put it, H0 states that ideal partner preference-matching "indeed have predictive power" regarding romantic evaluation.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48)</ref> put it, H0 states that ideal partner preference-matching "indeed have predictive power" regarding romantic evaluation.

text.text: Extending the baseline, the first hypothesis, H1, is based on the observation that background characteristics such as age and sex, as well as several scales of individual differences, operate as causally antecedent confounders of both attribute ratings as well as of the dependent measure itself (i.e., romantic evaluation).
Accordingly, H1 predicts that the inclusion of demographic and individualdifference covariates will produce significant effect sizes in the extended hierarchical regression analysis.

As the primary regression analysis conducted by Eastwick et al. (2024) is implemented in a bivariate trait-by-trait fashion, the second hypothesis, H2, posits that simultaneously entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes into a multivariate regression model will substantially attenuate all estimated coefficients relative to the Eastwick et al. (2024) estimates.
text.formatted: As the primary regression analysis conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> is implemented in a bivariate trait-by-trait fashion, the second hypothesis, H2, posits that simultaneously entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes into a multivariate regression model will substantially attenuate all estimated coefficients relative to the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> estimates.

text.text: Because rated attributes are intercorrelated, an attenuated effect would reflect inherent intertrait-confounding.
In other words, each trait-by-trait model is potentially confounded by either trait-specific mediation effects or causally antecedent mutual influences such as normative desirability standards.

Based on the methodological modification, the third hypothesis, H3, predicts that even after full hierarchical multivariate adjustment, idiosyncratic preference-matching effects will cluster near zero or turn insignificant.
This hypothesis is consistent with (at least) two theoretical arguments that cannot be distinguished within the utilized sample itself.

Either collider bias arising from conditioning on (most desired) partners constitutes a structural property of the sample that full multivariate regression adjustment cannot correct or the study-design itself is limited to detect idiosyncratic matching effects in the first place.

Together, H1, H2, and H3 test analytically two distinct components of the collider bias structure: what statistical adjustment can recover by properly incorporating all measured causally upstream variables; and where the sampling design imposes a ceiling on valid inference that no statistical model can compensate.
The thesis proceeds as follows.

Chapter 2 introduces directed acyclic graphs as a framework for causal reasoning and the mechanics of collider bias, before applying both to the specific causal structure of partner preference research in Chapter 3.

Chapter 4 translates this theoretical framework into a set of methodological implications for the Eastwick et al. (2024) research design and outlines the hierarchical multivariate extension developed in response.
text.formatted: Chapter 4 translates this theoretical framework into a set of methodological implications for the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> research design and outlines the hierarchical multivariate extension developed in response.

text.text: Chapter 5 describes the method, including the replication procedure, the model specification, and the analytical strategy.
Chapter 6 presents the results.
Chapter 7 discusses the findings in relation to the methodological framework and the broader implications for the preference-matching literature.

One solution to the causal inference problem in observational research described in the introduction is not to abandon the aspiration of causal claims altogether, but to make underlying assumptions explicit and formally transparent.

In this context, graphical causal models offer a "direct and powerful way of thinking about full causal systems and the strategies that can be used to estimate the effects within them" (Morgan & Winship, 2014, p. 77).
text.formatted: In this context, graphical causal models offer a "direct and powerful way of thinking about full causal systems and the strategies that can be used to estimate the effects within them" <ref type="bibr">(Morgan & Winship, 2014, p. 77)</ref>.

text.text: Directed acyclic graphs: framework for causal reasoning Developed primarily by computer scientist Judea Pearl (1985 Pearl ( , 1988 Pearl ( , 1993 Pearl ( , 1995 Pearl ( , 2000)), directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) have increasingly become synonymous with graphical causal models to provide "visual representations of qualitative causal assumptions" that "encode researchers' expert knowledge and beliefs about how the world works" (Elwert, 2013, p. 246).
text.formatted: Directed acyclic graphs: framework for causal reasoning Developed primarily by computer scientist Judea <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pearl (1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Pearl ( , 1988</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Pearl ( , 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Pearl ( , 1995</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Pearl ( , 2000))</ref>, directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) have increasingly become synonymous with graphical causal models to provide "visual representations of qualitative causal assumptions" that "encode researchers' expert knowledge and beliefs about how the world works" <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 246)</ref>.

text.text: DAGs are able to reveal what was otherwise omitted.
Informal theoretical commitments by researchers are thereby translated into a nonparametric graphical notation from which statistical implications can be systematically derived.

The nonparametric feature indicates that DAGs neither require a specific variable distribution (e.g., normal, Poisson), nor restrict the functional form of the direct effects such as linear, nonlinear etc. (Elwert, 2013, p. 248; Morgan & Winship, 2014, p. 94).
text.formatted: The nonparametric feature indicates that DAGs neither require a specific variable distribution (e.g., normal, Poisson), nor restrict the functional form of the direct effects such as linear, nonlinear etc. <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 248;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Morgan & Winship, 2014, p. 94)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, no magnitude of causal effects is assumed in the DAG framework.
The wide applicability is especially helpful to answer the question introduced in the previous section.
Concretely, " [w]hat third variables need to be controlled for?
text.formatted: Concretely, " <ref type="bibr">[w]</ref>hat third variables need to be controlled for?

text.text: Which third variables can be ignored?
And in which situations will statistical control worsen causal inference?"

text.text: Drawing from Elwert (2013, pp. 248-266), Morgan and Winship (2014, pp. 77-101), Pearl (2000, pp. 65-106), Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 35-52) and Rohrer (2018, pp. 27-40) the functionality of DAGs can be described as follows.
text.formatted: Drawing from <ref type="bibr">Elwert (2013, pp. 248-266)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Morgan and Winship (2014, pp. 77-101)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Pearl (2000, pp. 65-106)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 35-52)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Rohrer (2018, pp. 27-40)</ref> the functionality of DAGs can be described as follows.

text.text: A DAG consists of two basic elements: nodes (originally called 'vertices'), representing variables, and directed edges (i.e., single-headed arrows), representing direct causal effects.
An arrow from A to B asserts that a direct intervention on A would change B (in time).
Critically, missing arrows carry equal weight.
They encompass "the strong assumption of no direct causal effect between two variables for every member of the population", called the "strong null" hypothesis of no effect (Elwert, 2013, p. 248).
text.formatted: They encompass "the strong assumption of no direct causal effect between two variables for every member of the population", called the "strong null" hypothesis of no effect <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 248)</ref>.

text.text: This is a point that applied researchers often overlook.

As Elwert (2013, p. 248) insists, "in contrast to conventional social theory, which focuses on justifying what relationships do exist, DAGs insistently redirect the analyst's attention to justifying what arrows do not exist".
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Elwert (2013, p. 248)</ref> insists, "in contrast to conventional social theory, which focuses on justifying what relationships do exist, DAGs insistently redirect the analyst's attention to justifying what arrows do not exist".

text.text: It is precisely these "exclusion restrictions" that enable the identification of causal effects (Pearl, 2000, p. 101).
text.formatted: It is precisely these "exclusion restrictions" that enable the identification of causal effects <ref type="bibr">(Pearl, 2000, p. 101)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, adding arrows to an existing set of variables never helps to isolate the causal effect while adding variables might help.
DAGs are acyclic by design, meaning no variable can be its own ancestor.
This enforces temporal consistency: the future cannot cause the past.
To address variables that influence themselves in a different point in time, the temporal order is explicitly considered by adding another variable indicating repeated measurement.
Childhood intelligence, for instance, will likely influence intelligence measured as an adult.
Consequently, intelligence is split up into childhood and adult intelligence depicted as two separate nodes (variables) within the same DAG.
Despite the fact that any data-generating process can become increasingly complex, causal models can be decomposed into three elementary causal structures.
Firstly, a chain in the form of X → Z → Y transmits a genuine causal effect from X to Y through Z, whereas X, Y and Z can represent either single variables or a set of multiple variables.
In this context, a single variable Z is called a mediator variable for it mediates a causal effect of interest from X to Y.
Mediator variables should generally not be controlled for to account for their causal function within the chain formation.

There are exceptions, such as estimating the direct effect of X on Y by mediation analysis (for an introduction, as well as the distinction of mediator and moderator variables, see Baron & Kenny, 1986; Hayes, 2017; Rohrer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: There are exceptions, such as estimating the direct effect of X on Y by mediation analysis (for an introduction, as well as the distinction of mediator and moderator variables, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Baron & Kenny, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hayes, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Rohrer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, controlling for mediator variables usually leads to overcontrol bias and potential underestimation of the causal effect of X on Y (Rohrer, 2018, p. 38).
text.formatted: However, controlling for mediator variables usually leads to overcontrol bias and potential underestimation of the causal effect of X on Y <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 38)</ref>.

text.text: The second elementary structure is called fork, depicted as X ← Z → Y, and generates a so called spurious (i.e., non-causal) association between X and Y through their common cause Z, introducing the canonical structure of confounding.
If potentially confounding variables are unobserved (i.e., unmeasured), they are typically denoted by U (Elwert, 2013, p. 249).
text.formatted: If potentially confounding variables are unobserved (i.e., unmeasured), they are typically denoted by U <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 249)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, common-cause confounding by an unobserved variable is represented graphically by a bi-headed dashed arrow between the affected variables (Rohrer, 2018, p. 29).
text.formatted: In some cases, common-cause confounding by an unobserved variable is represented graphically by a bi-headed dashed arrow between the affected variables <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 29)</ref>.

text.text: Idiosyncratic factors that affect only a single node and have no effect on any other variable are usually omitted from the graphical representation.
Such factors are conceptualized as exogenous non-common causes or independent error terms and generally do not affect causal associations because they do not open additional paths between variables.
Lastly, an inverted fork in the form of X → Z ← Y, represents the structure of a common effect.
Z in this case is called collider variable and caused by both X and Y (i.e., two arrows are pointing in Z).
Crucially, in an unconditional analysis, Z blocks the path and induces no association between X and Y. The inverted fork structure is examined in more detail in the next section.

As Elwert (2013, p. 249) summarizes, "these [three] structures correspond exactly to causation, confounding, and endogenous selection" which represent the only sources of observable association in any dataset.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Elwert (2013, p. 249)</ref> summarizes, "these [three] structures correspond exactly to causation, confounding, and endogenous selection" which represent the only sources of observable association in any dataset.

text.text: However, causal models are usually comprised of a large variety of these elementary structures.
In this context, causal and noncausal (spurious) paths are distinguished in the following way.
A causal path is one along which all arrows point consistently away from the exposure and toward the outcome.
This corresponds with a (multiple) chain and thus transmits a genuine causal effect.
A noncausal path contains at least one arrow pointing in the opposite direction.
It may still transmit statistical association, but that association does not represent a causal effect.

In this sense, a causal DAG is defined as a DAG that "include[s] all common measured and unmeasured causes of any pair of variables" (Spirtes et al., 1993 (Spirtes et al., /2001;; cited in Elwert, 2013, p. 249).
text.formatted: In this sense, a causal DAG is defined as a DAG that "include[s] all common measured and unmeasured causes of any pair of variables" <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Spirtes et al., 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Spirtes et al., /2001;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">cited in Elwert, 2013, p. 249)</ref>.

text.text: This rather "bold claim" needs to be carefully investigated and tested "against the data as far as possible" (Elwert, 2013, p. 249).
text.formatted: This rather "bold claim" needs to be carefully investigated and tested "against the data as far as possible" <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 249)</ref>.

text.text: Concerning terminology, variables which are directly caused by a given variable are called children while variables directly or indirectly caused by a given variable are called its descendants.
Vice versa, direct causes of a variable are called parents, and all direct and indirect causes of a variable are called ancestors.
The formal tool that unifies all three elementary structures is d-separation, which was introduced by Pearl (1988).
text.formatted: The formal tool that unifies all three elementary structures is d-separation, which was introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Pearl (1988)</ref>.

text.text: D-separation is a graphical criterion for determining when a path between two variables transmits association and when it is blocked.
In other words, d-separation indicates whether two variables are likely dependent or definitely independent (Pearl et al., 2016, p. 46).
text.formatted: In other words, d-separation indicates whether two variables are likely dependent or definitely independent <ref type="bibr">(Pearl et al., 2016, p. 46)</ref>.

text.text: A path is d-separated (i.e., blocked) if it contains either a conditioned non-collider (a confounder or mediator that has been controlled for) or an unconditioned collider (an inverted fork that has not been controlled for).

A path is otherwise d-connected (i.e., open, unblocked). Pearl et al. (2016, p. 36) correspondingly demonstrate that the structure of a causal graph, combined with observational data, makes it possible "to predict quantitatively the results of interventions without actually performing them".
text.formatted: A path is otherwise d-connected (i.e., open, unblocked). <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, p. 36)</ref> correspondingly demonstrate that the structure of a causal graph, combined with observational data, makes it possible "to predict quantitatively the results of interventions without actually performing them".

text.text: Those assumptions lead to the backdoor criterion (Pearl, 1993).
text.formatted: Those assumptions lead to the backdoor criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Pearl, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: A set of variables Z satisfies the backdoor criterion for the causal effect of exposure X on outcome Y if Z blocks (i.e., closes) every non-causal backdoor path (i.e., every path that enters Y with an arrow) while containing no descendant of X (Pearl, 1993; Pearl, 2000, p. 79).
text.formatted: A set of variables Z satisfies the backdoor criterion for the causal effect of exposure X on outcome Y if Z blocks (i.e., closes) every non-causal backdoor path (i.e., every path that enters Y with an arrow) while containing no descendant of X <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Pearl, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pearl, 2000, p. 79)</ref>.

text.text: The transmission of an association is thus cut by statistically controlling a node, the purpose of the statistical control of third variables which was introduced in the previous chapter.
If such a set Z exists and is measured, the causal effect of X on Y can explicitly be determined from observational data.

For an introduction of various control practices, such as stratification, adjustment (i.e., conditioning on or controlling for a third variable in regression analysis) and matching, see Rohrer (2018, pp. 32-33).
text.formatted: For an introduction of various control practices, such as stratification, adjustment (i.e., conditioning on or controlling for a third variable in regression analysis) and matching, see <ref type="bibr">Rohrer (2018, pp. 32-33)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note, that a variable that is statistically associated with both exposure and outcome is not necessarily a confounder for it may instead be a collider.
Indicated by the inverted fork structure, controlling for it actively induces collider bias, as will be investigated in the next section.
Finally, causality is always "conditional on the validity of the stated causal model" (Elwert, 2013, p. 247).
text.formatted: Finally, causality is always "conditional on the validity of the stated causal model" <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 247)</ref>.

text.text: As Kaltenpoth (2024, p. 15) notes, "many processes with different causal relationships are consistent with the observed distribution".
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Kaltenpoth (2024, p. 15)</ref> notes, "many processes with different causal relationships are consistent with the observed distribution".

text.text: Consequently, the DAG does not eliminate the need for theoretical commitments.
Rather, it makes those commitments visible and refutable against the data to the extent that their implications are empirically accessible.
In this sense, assumptions "cannot be corrected unless they are noticed and understood" (Elwert, 2013, p. 270).
text.formatted: In this sense, assumptions "cannot be corrected unless they are noticed and understood" <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 270)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, Rohrer (2018, p. 31) concludes that "the assumption that one has correctly captured the causal web and successfully blocked all back-door paths is in most cases a very strong one, because it posits that no relevant variables have been omitted from the causal graph.
text.formatted: Moreover, <ref type="bibr">Rohrer (2018, p. 31)</ref> concludes that "the assumption that one has correctly captured the causal web and successfully blocked all back-door paths is in most cases a very strong one, because it posits that no relevant variables have been omitted from the causal graph.

text.text: Whether this is plausible or not needs to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis".

As indicated in the introduction, of the three structural sources of association identified in the previous section, collider variables play a crucial role for being intellectually less accessible and potentially elusive (Pearl et al., 2016 , p. 41, Rohrer, 2018, p. 35).
text.formatted: As indicated in the introduction, of the three structural sources of association identified in the previous section, collider variables play a crucial role for being intellectually less accessible and potentially elusive <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Pearl et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr">, p. 41, Rohrer, 2018, p. 35)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, collider bias can occur at any stage of the research process, due to conditioning on an outcome, one of its descendants, intermediate variables, and even pretreatment variables (Elwert, 2013, p. 262).
text.formatted: Moreover, collider bias can occur at any stage of the research process, due to conditioning on an outcome, one of its descendants, intermediate variables, and even pretreatment variables <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 262)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, two steps are required in order for bias to be avoided: "First, one must be aware of the collider variable, and second, one must be able to run analyses that are not conditional on the collider" (Rohrer, 2018, p. 36).
text.formatted: Crucially, two steps are required in order for bias to be avoided: "First, one must be aware of the collider variable, and second, one must be able to run analyses that are not conditional on the collider" <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 36)</ref>.

text.text: The second step, however, presupposes that the collider variable has been measured (Kaltenpoth, 2024, p. 114).
text.formatted: The second step, however, presupposes that the collider variable has been measured <ref type="bibr">(Kaltenpoth, 2024, p. 114)</ref>.

text.text: The DAG framework is especially supportive in increasing awareness and shows that conditioning on a collider proves systematically wrong in structural configurations of inverted forks (i.e., X → Z ← Y).
The critical feature of colliders, derived from d-separation, is their asymmetric behavior under conditioning.
As mentioned, without conditioning, a collider blocks the path between its parents.
As Pearl et al. (2016, p. 41) demonstrate, X and Y are dependent conditional on Z even when X and Y are unconditionally independent.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, p. 41</ref>) demonstrate, X and Y are dependent conditional on Z even when X and Y are unconditionally independent.

text.text: This leads to the introduction of "unknown amounts of bias into the estimate of the total causal effect […] which was, in fact, correctly estimated when we did not control for them" (Kaltenpoth, 2024, p. 4).
text.formatted: This leads to the introduction of "unknown amounts of bias into the estimate of the total causal effect […] which was, in fact, correctly estimated when we did not control for them" <ref type="bibr">(Kaltenpoth, 2024, p. 4</ref>).

text.text: The reversal from independence to conditional dependence is essentially the definition of collider bias.

In the DAG framework, these conditional or spurious association between X and Y are indicated by a dashed line without arrowheads (X---Y, sometimes also depicted as bi-headed arrows, Elwert, 2013, p. 250).
text.formatted: In the DAG framework, these conditional or spurious association between X and Y are indicated by a dashed line without arrowheads (X---Y, sometimes also depicted as bi-headed arrows, <ref type="bibr">Elwert, 2013, p. 250)</ref>.

text.text: Corresponding biases potentially increase when measurement error of third variables is taken into account.

This issue is not further discussed in the paper, however, according to Westfall and Yarkoni (2016, p. 1) "the false positive rate can reach very high levels, approaching almost 100%" and counterintuitively "increases when sample sizes are large".
There are many different terms for collider bias.

It has been labelled collider stratification bias (Greenland, 2003), selection bias (Hernán et al., 2004), endogenous selection bias (Elwert & Winship, 2014), Berkson's (1946) bias, explaining away effect (Kim & Pearl, 1983) or conditioning bias (Morgan & Winship, 2007).
text.formatted: It has been labelled collider stratification bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Greenland, 2003)</ref>, selection bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hernán et al., 2004)</ref>, endogenous selection bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Elwert & Winship, 2014</ref>), <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Berkson's (1946)</ref> bias, explaining away effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kim & Pearl, 1983)</ref> or conditioning bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Morgan & Winship, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Recently, Lu et al. (2023, pp. 407-408) further differentiated collider bias by distinguishing between collider restriction bias and collider adjustment bias.
text.formatted: Recently, <ref type="bibr">Lu et al. (2023, pp. 407-408)</ref> further differentiated collider bias by distinguishing between collider restriction bias and collider adjustment bias.

text.text: The first form occurs when analysis is restricted to a subgroup defined by a collider (or its descendant; including stratification of subgroups while separately reporting the results).
In this way, collider restriction bias usually "results from the sampling procedure" (Rohrer, 2018, p. 36).
text.formatted: In this way, collider restriction bias usually "results from the sampling procedure" <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 36)</ref>.

text.text: The latter bias is induced through inclusion of a collider (or its descendant) in a regression model.

In this sense collider restriction bias can be treated as a form of (endogenous) selection bias while collider adjustment bias is rather understood as a specific overadjustment bias (Lu et al., 2021; Schisterman et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In this sense collider restriction bias can be treated as a form of (endogenous) selection bias while collider adjustment bias is rather understood as a specific overadjustment bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lu et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Schisterman et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, several special cases of collider bias exist such as survivorship bias (Hudomiet et al., 2021), sample truncation bias (Hausman & Wise, 1977), non-response bias (Lin et al., 1999), ascertainment bias (Elwert & Winship, 2014), attrition bias (Rohrer, 2018, p. 36) and Heckman (1974 Heckman ( , 1979) ) selection bias.
text.formatted: Furthermore, several special cases of collider bias exist such as survivorship bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hudomiet et al., 2021)</ref>, sample truncation bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hausman & Wise, 1977)</ref>, non-response bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lin et al., 1999)</ref>, ascertainment bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Elwert & Winship, 2014)</ref>, attrition bias <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 36)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Heckman (1974</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Heckman ( , 1979) )</ref> selection bias.

text.text: For a comprehensive systematic review of collider bias terminology and more detailed distinctions, see Levy (2023).
text.formatted: For a comprehensive systematic review of collider bias terminology and more detailed distinctions, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Levy (2023)</ref>.

text.text: The conclusion, however, reveals that, despite few specific exceptions, "all selection bias is collider bias" (Levy, 2023, p. 296).
text.formatted: The conclusion, however, reveals that, despite few specific exceptions, "all selection bias is collider bias" <ref type="bibr">(Levy, 2023, p. 296)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of this paper, the distinction of Lu et al. (2023) is adopted, nonetheless, the remedy to both biases is similarly "not to condition on such variables" (Elwert, 2013, p. 252).
text.formatted: In the context of this paper, the distinction of <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lu et al. (2023)</ref> is adopted, nonetheless, the remedy to both biases is similarly "not to condition on such variables" <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, p. 252)</ref>.

text.text: Though cautious of overcontrol bias, this paper's focus lies on collider restriction bias.

The mechanism becomes concrete through example. Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 41-42) illustrate it with a scholarship scheme that awards places to students who are either musically talented (X) or academically high-achieving (Y).
text.formatted: The mechanism becomes concrete through example. <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 41-42)</ref> illustrate it with a scholarship scheme that awards places to students who are either musically talented (X) or academically high-achieving (Y).

text.text: In the general population, musical talent and academic achievement may be wholly uncorrelated.
Yet if one restricts analysis to scholarship recipients (Z), and thus conditions on a collider, a spurious negative association emerges without any causal effect.

Among recipients, a student with low academic achievement implies high musical talent in average, and vice versa. Pearl et al. (2016, p. 41) propose to understand conditioning on a third variable as "filtering by the value of the conditioning variable".
text.formatted: Among recipients, a student with low academic achievement implies high musical talent in average, and vice versa. <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, p. 41)</ref> propose to understand conditioning on a third variable as "filtering by the value of the conditioning variable".

text.text: In this sense, by conditioning on Z, comparisons to cases in which Z takes the same value are limited.

For the value of Z depends on X and Y (i.e., common effect), comparing cases where Z takes a specific value are compensated in the way that any change in the value of X must account for a change in the value of Y.
Otherwise, the value of Z would likewise have to change, which is impossible while controlling for it.

After all, this mechanism induces a spurious correlation between X and Y. To put it generally, this procedure implies the "nonrepresentativeness of samples" which is often overlooked in scientific research (Rohrer, 2018, p. 36).
text.formatted: After all, this mechanism induces a spurious correlation between X and Y. To put it generally, this procedure implies the "nonrepresentativeness of samples" which is often overlooked in scientific research <ref type="bibr">(Rohrer, 2018, p. 36)</ref>.

text.text: The exemplified issue intensifies for "selecting on a collider always leads to bias, but this bias may not occur in the stratum that coincides with our analytical sample" (Levy, 2023, p. 105).
text.formatted: The exemplified issue intensifies for "selecting on a collider always leads to bias, but this bias may not occur in the stratum that coincides with our analytical sample" <ref type="bibr">(Levy, 2023, p. 105)</ref>.

text.text: This essentially means, that causal distortions due to collider bias may be invisible within the restricted dataset itself, detectable only from a point outside of it.
If the analytical sample is itself defined by conditioning on a collider, the bias becomes structural, not statistical.
The primary remedy in this case is the reconstitution of the sample.

If this is not possible, however, spurious effects can be mitigated by conscientiously closing corresponding backdoor paths (Elwert, 2013, pp. 256-257; Hernán et al., 2004, pp. 620-621; Shpitser et al., 2010, p. 530).
text.formatted: If this is not possible, however, spurious effects can be mitigated by conscientiously closing corresponding backdoor paths <ref type="bibr">(Elwert, 2013, pp. 256-257;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hernán et al., 2004, pp. 620-621;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shpitser et al., 2010, p. 530)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, the practice of making causal inferences on the basis of observational data "depends crucially on awareness" (Rohrer, 2018, p. 38).
