text.text: Building on the theoretical explanations of the previous chapter, the aim of this section is to introduce the research field of partner preference research to exemplify potential collider restriction bias effects in the data collection as well as analysis process.
A long-standing question in relationship research is whether people actually end up with partners who match what they say they want (Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1).
text.formatted: A long-standing question in relationship research is whether people actually end up with partners who match what they say they want <ref type="bibr">(Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: When asked, people tend to describe their ideal romantic partner in terms of attributes (i.e., traits) like physical attractiveness, warmth, intelligence, or financial security (Buss, 1989; Eagly & Wood, 1999; Eastwick et al., 2014; Fletcher et al., 1999; Hill, 1945).
text.formatted: When asked, people tend to describe their ideal romantic partner in terms of attributes (i.e., traits) like physical attractiveness, warmth, intelligence, or financial security <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Buss, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Eagly & Wood, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Eastwick et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fletcher et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hill, 1945)</ref>.

text.text: These so-called ideal partner preferences are frequently utilized to examine the corresponding preference-matching hypothesis as described in the Introduction.

Based on the observation, that positive evaluation of romantic partners is a key predictor of health and mortality (Robles et al., 2014), its assumption is central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model (Fletcher et al., 1999), which proposes that people incorporate ideal personality traits when evaluating both potential and current partners (Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 2).
text.formatted: Based on the observation, that positive evaluation of romantic partners is a key predictor of health and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Robles et al., 2014)</ref>, its assumption is central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fletcher et al., 1999)</ref>, which proposes that people incorporate ideal personality traits when evaluating both potential and current partners <ref type="bibr">(Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 2)</ref>.

text.text: Despite decades of research, empirical support for the matching hypotheses is surprisingly "murky" (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5).
text.formatted: Despite decades of research, empirical support for the matching hypotheses is surprisingly "murky" <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, concerns of causal inference in this research field remain largely untackled (Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485; Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1).
text.formatted: Moreover, concerns of causal inference in this research field remain largely untackled <ref type="bibr">(Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: As mentioned in the introduction, Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 43) conducted the most comprehensive investigation of preference-matching to date.
text.formatted: As mentioned in the introduction, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 43)</ref> conducted the most comprehensive investigation of preference-matching to date.

text.text: Partnering with the Psychological Science Accelerator (PSA), they collected data from N = 10,358 participants across 43 countries and 22 languages.
Individuals in established romantic relationships as well as single individuals (who evaluated the person they most desired as a partner) took part.
The primary planned analyses used multilevel models that accounted for the nesting of participants within the 60 samples which have been included in the dataset.

All participants similarly rated 35 partner attributes in terms of their ideal preferences and then rated their (most desired) partner on the same attributes, before reporting a romantic evaluation of that person as the dependent measure (by answering six questions such as: 'I am romantically interested in…').

The attributes covered a range of normatively desirable traits, including physical attractiveness, personality traits, and relational qualities, as well as four negatively worded Big Five items (e.g., critical, quarrelsome; anxious, easily upset).
The full list of attributes is presented in Table 1 in the Result section.
text.formatted: The full list of attributes is presented in Table <ref type="table">1</ref> in the Result section.

text.text: This design allowed the authors to test the preference-matching hypothesis using four distinct analytic approaches of varying methodological rigor.

These analytical approaches resulted from a systematic review performed by Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 6) themselves and is supposed to comprise the whole methodological spectrum of the literature of partner preference matching.
text.formatted: These analytical approaches resulted from a systematic review performed by <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 6)</ref> themselves and is supposed to comprise the whole methodological spectrum of the literature of partner preference matching.

text.text: The following explanations of each approach are based on Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 6-8).
text.formatted: The following explanations of each approach are based on <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 6-8)</ref>.

text.text: Ideal-trait correlations (ITC) simply examine whether participants who rate a particular trait as more desirable also perceive their partner as higher on that trait.

Measured by the standardized regression coefficient, this test reveals moderate average effect sizes of β = .33 but is especially susceptible to alternative explanations for it lacks a dependent measure; e.g., attraction or romantic evaluation (Conroy-Beam & Buss, 2016, p. 8; Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 6; Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 2).
text.formatted: Measured by the standardized regression coefficient, this test reveals moderate average effect sizes of β = .33 but is especially susceptible to alternative explanations for it lacks a dependent measure; e.g., attraction or romantic evaluation <ref type="bibr">(Conroy-Beam & Buss, 2016, p. 8;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 6;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gerlach et al., 2019, p.</ref> 2).

text.text: The raw pattern metric (RPM) computes a within-person correlation across all 35 attributes between a participant's ideal ratings and their partner attribute ratings.
This yields a single index of how well the partner matches the participant's profile of preferences.
It is subsequently normalized and used to predict the evaluative outcome of romantic attraction.

While this approach tends to produce substantial effect sizes (β = .37 in the full sample), it is confounded with the normative desirability of traits (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 7; Rogers et al., 2018; Wood & Furr, 2016).
text.formatted: While this approach tends to produce substantial effect sizes (β = .37 in the full sample), it is confounded with the normative desirability of traits <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 7;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Rogers et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Wood & Furr, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Partners perceived as having more positive traits will receive higher scores on this metric regardless of whether those traits specifically match the participant's stated priorities.

Consequently, the corrected pattern metric (CPM) addresses this confound by mean-centering both ideal and attribute ratings at the sample level before computing the withinperson correlation (Eastwick et al., 2019 (Eastwick et al., , 2024, p. 6;, p. 6; Fletcher et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Consequently, the corrected pattern metric (CPM) addresses this confound by mean-centering both ideal and attribute ratings at the sample level before computing the withinperson correlation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Eastwick et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., , 2024, p. 6;, p. 6;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fletcher et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This (supposedly) removes the shared normative component, so that only idiosyncratic matching accounts for the effect (i.e., the degree to which a person's unique preference profile matches their partner's unique trait profile). Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 28) report a corrected pattern metric effect of β = .19 in the full sample.
text.formatted: This (supposedly) removes the shared normative component, so that only idiosyncratic matching accounts for the effect (i.e., the degree to which a person's unique preference profile matches their partner's unique trait profile). <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 28)</ref> report a corrected pattern metric effect of β = .19 in the full sample.

text.text: Finally, the level metric (LM) refers to the trait-by-trait interaction between a participant's ideal for and their partner's rating on that trait, predicting romantic evaluation while controlling for both main effects (i.e., participant's ideal and partner's traits).
This test asks, for each trait separately, whether the attributeevaluation association is stronger among participants who place greater importance on that trait.
As an illustration, suppose that perceiving a partner as humorous is positively related to attraction toward that partner.
The level metric examines whether this relationship is stronger among individuals who place greater importance on humor in an ideal partner than among those who consider humor less important.
In other words, it assesses whether people with stronger preferences for a particular trait assign greater evaluative significance to that trait when judging their partners.
After all, average level metric interaction effects were very small.

The average interaction term was β = .04 across all 35 traits, and effects for normatively highly desirable traits such as attractive or considerate were essentially zero (Eastwick et al., 2024, pp. 28-29).
text.formatted: The average interaction term was β = .04 across all 35 traits, and effects for normatively highly desirable traits such as attractive or considerate were essentially zero <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, pp. 28-29)</ref>.

text.text: While Eastwick et al. (2024) do not report any main effects, the results reveal that attraction to these partners is driven almost entirely by participant's ideal and partner's traits rather than idiosyncratic weighting (i.e., interaction).
text.formatted: While <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> do not report any main effects, the results reveal that attraction to these partners is driven almost entirely by participant's ideal and partner's traits rather than idiosyncratic weighting (i.e., interaction).

text.text: Moreover, following an approach proposed by Sparks et al. (2020), Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 13) asked participants to nominate and rate additional peer targets of their preferred gender.
text.formatted: Moreover, following an approach proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Sparks et al. (2020)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 13)</ref> asked participants to nominate and rate additional peer targets of their preferred gender.

text.text: Their primary analysis, however, incorporated the evaluation of the (most desired) partner only, as it was preregistered in their analysis plan.
Overall, Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48) concluded that (idiosyncratic) preference-matching effects exist but are modest in size and highly dependent on how they are measured.
text.formatted: Overall, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48)</ref> concluded that (idiosyncratic) preference-matching effects exist but are modest in size and highly dependent on how they are measured.

text.text: The study is notable for its scale, its preregistered design, and the transparent availability of data and analysis code.
At the same time, the study raises a number of methodological concerns which will be shown in the next section.
The theoretical groundwork for the central structural flaws in partner preference research has been established in the preceding two chapters.

Stated in DAG terminology presented in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, the problem is straightforward: ideal partner preferences and the partner's actual attributes (rated by participants themselves) are both causes of relationship formation.
Relationship formation is therefore a common effect or collider variable on the path between ideals and partner traits (ideal preferences → relationship formation ← partner attributes).
As Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 6) themselves acknowledge, "the selection event is not used as a measured variable (i.e., there are no 'unselected' partners)".
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 6</ref>) themselves acknowledge, "the selection event is not used as a measured variable (i.e., there are no 'unselected' partners)".

text.text: Notably, Eastwick et al. (2024) state this observation specifically in relation to ideal-trait correlations.
text.formatted: Notably, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> state this observation specifically in relation to ideal-trait correlations.

text.text: The structural problem, however, equally concerns level metric and the corrected pattern metric.

As mentioned above, Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 13) applied a study design which deliberately includes single participants (who rate their most desired partner) to address the issue of relationship status.
text.formatted: As mentioned above, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 13</ref>) applied a study design which deliberately includes single participants (who rate their most desired partner) to address the issue of relationship status.

text.text: They report multiple times that differences of partnered and single participants tended to be "very small" (Eastwick et al., 2024, pp. 25, 28, 30).
text.formatted: They report multiple times that differences of partnered and single participants tended to be "very small" <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, pp. 25, 28, 30)</ref>.

text.text: While other explanations might be possible, this finding can be read as a hint that replacing established by most desired partners has no mitigating effect on collider restriction bias.
In other words, established as well as most desired relationships both imply conditioning on a mutual collider variable of high romantic evaluation.
The DAG in Figure 1  with the effect of collider restriction bias itself.
text.formatted: The DAG in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>  with the effect of collider restriction bias itself.

text.text: The analysis proceeds by distinguishing three different layers as shown in Figure 1.

To improve clarity and reduce the number of arrows displayed, variables with the same function are grouped together into three main segments and framed in dashed lines: Potentially spurious associations based on conditioning on (most desired) partners are indicated by biheaded dashed arrows as introduced in Section 2.1.

Note that even though all single variables within and between the three segments are ancestors of the collider variable and might consequently be spuriously correlated, not all such associations are explicitly drawn to increase visibility.
The depicted graph as such is thus no DAG in a classical sense but rather provides an overview of corresponding variables and associations of the full empirical model.
With Figure 2, which is presented below, a more detailed description of single variables will be provided.
text.formatted: With Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>, which is presented below, a more detailed description of single variables will be provided.

text.text: Note.
Variables with the same causal function are grouped into three dashed-bordered segments: At the top layer, a cluster of measured covariates is presented.
Those were integrated into the survey conducted by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Those were integrated into the survey conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: They include certain variables on demographics, such as age, gender and sexual orientation, as well as on individual difference measures, such as individualism/ collectivism and relational mobility scales.
Importantly the segment also contains a separate node representing unmeasured confounders (U) which have not been included in the analysis (e.g., subjective well-being at the time of participation).
All of these variables causally precede both sets of variables of interest.
Their arrows toward both ideal preferences and partner attributes indicate that these background factors are common causes of both, opening genuine backdoor paths between them.
At the same time, they potentially influence the romantic evaluation itself.

Variables of the first segment thus follow a confounding structure, not a collider structure: it is independent of the selection event and requires statistical adjustment to be neutralized, provided the relevant variables have been measured.

The first layer of the DAG corresponds with the first hypothesis stated in the introduction (H1) and serves as the basis for investigating if measured individual background criteria have a confounding effect over and above main and interaction effects. Eastwick et al. (2024) indirectly control for some of these unmeasured confounders by applying the multilevel structure described in Chapter 3.
text.formatted: The first layer of the DAG corresponds with the first hypothesis stated in the introduction (H1) and serves as the basis for investigating if measured individual background criteria have a confounding effect over and above main and interaction effects. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> indirectly control for some of these unmeasured confounders by applying the multilevel structure described in Chapter 3.

text.text: Culture-dependent third variable influences are partly covered by the variance of varying effects. Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 22) reported relatively small differences in the evaluation of romantic evaluation of about 3% variance across samples (varying intercept) and 0.6 % variance accounting for varying slopes of each partner attribute rating.
text.formatted: Culture-dependent third variable influences are partly covered by the variance of varying effects. <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 22)</ref> reported relatively small differences in the evaluation of romantic evaluation of about 3% variance across samples (varying intercept) and 0.6 % variance accounting for varying slopes of each partner attribute rating.

text.text: In the present multilevel context, the varying intercept captures the degree to which the average level of romantic evaluation differs systematically across the 60 laboratory samples.
This reflects, for instance, culturally specific baseline tendencies toward positive or reserved partner evaluation.
The varying slope, by contrast, captures the degree to which the association between a given partner attribute and romantic evaluation differs across samples.
That is, whether perceiving a partner as, say, humorous predicts romantic evaluation more strongly in some cultural contexts than others.

That both components account for less than 4% of total variance combined indicates that neither baseline romantic evaluation nor the evaluative weight assigned to specific partner attributes varies substantially across cultures.

The preference-matching structure is thus broadly consistent across the 60 samples, suggesting that the methodological concerns raised in the present thesis generalize beyond any single cultural context rather than being confined to specific subsamples.
At the second layer, ideal preferences and partner attributes are each depicted as clusters of variables connected by dashed bidirectional arrows within their respective groups.

While these arrows are usually used to show the impact of spurious associations based on conditioning on a collider (see Section 2.2), they may as well indicate common-cause confounding by unobserved variables (see Section 2.1; Rohrer, 2018, p. 29).
text.formatted: While these arrows are usually used to show the impact of spurious associations based on conditioning on a collider (see Section 2.2), they may as well indicate common-cause confounding by unobserved variables (see Section 2.1; <ref type="bibr">Rohrer, 2018, p. 29)</ref>.

text.text: The second aspect will be discussed first for it affects the analysis irrespective of collider restriction bias which will be discussed afterwards.
Within-cluster associations in this case capture at least two distinct phenomena: intertrait confounding and halo effects.
Attributes rated in the Eastwick et al. (2024) participants survey are highly correlated among ideals as well as partner trait ratings.
text.formatted: Attributes rated in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> participants survey are highly correlated among ideals as well as partner trait ratings.

text.text: Participants who strongly value intelligence for instance, tend also to positively value humor (to pick another example).

Attribute ratings in this case are in large parts driven by (unknown) mediating effects between corresponding variables or by shared background factors such as normative desirability standards or general positive orientation (indicated by the U node).

Especially among partner attributes, they additionally reflect halo effects where global positive evaluations of targets (e.g., high relationship satisfaction or sympathy) artificially inflate the rating of specific individual attributes (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977).
text.formatted: Especially among partner attributes, they additionally reflect halo effects where global positive evaluations of targets (e.g., high relationship satisfaction or sympathy) artificially inflate the rating of specific individual attributes <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Nisbett & Wilson, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: A (most desired) partner perceived as highly attractive for instance is likely to be rated as more intelligent or humorous, regardless of whether these traits are objectively related.
For now, both phenomena are still forms of confounding rather than collider restriction bias, because they arise from shared common causes rather than from conditioning on a selection event.
They represent open backdoor paths in the causal graph that the trait-by-trait level metric does not close.
A more detailed exemplification is provided in Panel A in Figure 2.
text.formatted: A more detailed exemplification is provided in Panel A in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>.

text.text: The second layer corresponds with the second hypothesis (H2) as stated in the introduction and captures if simultaneously entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes into a multivariate regression model will substantially attenuate the estimated coefficients relative to the Eastwick et al. (2024) analysis.
text.formatted: The second layer corresponds with the second hypothesis (H2) as stated in the introduction and captures if simultaneously entering all 35 ideal preferences and partner attributes into a multivariate regression model will substantially attenuate the estimated coefficients relative to the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> analysis.

text.text: The first two layers and hypotheses thus represent concerns which are basically analysis-related, rather than sample or study-design related.

As depicted in the DAG in Figure 1, all three clusters are then causally associated with the romantic evaluation in the third layer, which in turn causes the selection event of becoming the (most desired) partner.
text.formatted: As depicted in the DAG in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>, all three clusters are then causally associated with the romantic evaluation in the third layer, which in turn causes the selection event of becoming the (most desired) partner.

text.text: The direction of these causal assumptions is as such debatable.

The so-called 'relationship formation hypothesis', for instance, offers a reverse-causality explanation by suggesting that partner ideals may be shaped by existing relationships (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 20).
text.formatted: The so-called 'relationship formation hypothesis', for instance, offers a reverse-causality explanation by suggesting that partner ideals may be shaped by existing relationships <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 20)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, individuals may modify their ideal preferences to correspond more closely to their current partner's attributes, rather than choosing partners who already match their previously held ideals (Gerlach et al., 2019; Neff & Karney, 2003).
text.formatted: Specifically, individuals may modify their ideal preferences to correspond more closely to their current partner's attributes, rather than choosing partners who already match their previously held ideals <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gerlach et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Neff & Karney, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Reverse causality as a further distinct methodological phenomenon, though no focus of this thesis, is briefly picked up in the next section.
However, conditioning on (most desired) partners, as every study using established couples or most desired partner ratings necessarily does, activates the collider mechanism described in Section 2.2.
This adds an additional layer of spurious covariance between ideal preferences and partner attributes on top of the pre-existing confounding issues described above.
To use the same terminology as above, corresponding concerns are rather sample-related than analysis or study design-related.
Figure 2 makes explicit that the (most desired) partner node is not merely a sampling criterion but an active part of the causal structure.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> makes explicit that the (most desired) partner node is not merely a sampling criterion but an active part of the causal structure.

text.text: The analysis is embedded in a world where high romantic evaluation is given by construction.

This structural fact distorts estimated associations throughout: participants with high ideals and objectively low-scoring partners must still have high romantic evaluations to justify their status as (most desired) partners itself.
In other words, high romantic evaluations are the condition for being in the sample in the first place.
The resulting 'upward pressure' on perceived partner trait ratings that follows is not deliberate misreporting; it is a structural artifact of collider conditioning.
This dynamic is an essential reason why intertrait confounding and halo effects are exacerbated when conditioning on the sample-restricting collider.
Note.

Panel A illustrating intertrait confounding and collider restriction bias through a simplified threevariable example involving ideal humor preference, perceived partner humor, and perceived partner intelligence.
Panel B depicts the analytical structure of the level metric, including an explicit Interactions node representing the 35 Ideal × PartnerAttribute product terms.
Bidirectional dashed arrows indicate spurious associations.
U = unmeasured confounders.
Panel A in Figure 2 introduces the fundamental structural problem of the inverted fork structure through a simplified example involving three variables.
text.formatted: Panel A in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> introduces the fundamental structural problem of the inverted fork structure through a simplified example involving three variables.

text.text: To exemplarily repeat, the participant's ideal preference for humor and their ratings of the partner's humor and intelligence are potentially independent causes of the participant's romantic evaluation of that partner.
Romantic evaluation is therefore a collider in the sense of Section 2.1.

As d-separation implies conditioning on a collider or any of its descendants opens the paths between the collider's parent variables, inducing spurious statistical associations where no direct causal relationship exists.
In Panel A, this mechanism is indicated by the dashed bidirectional arrows connecting the ideal humor preference, the perceived partner humor, and the perceived partner intelligence.
Within the restricted sample, these three variables are forced into mutual dependence.

The logic is parallel to the scholarship scheme of Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 41-42) introduced in Section 2.2: a participant whose ideal for humor is high but whose partner scores poorly on humor must somehow maintain a sufficiently high romantic evaluation to have entered the sample.
text.formatted: The logic is parallel to the scholarship scheme of <ref type="bibr">Pearl et al. (2016, pp. 41-42)</ref> introduced in Section 2.2: a participant whose ideal for humor is high but whose partner scores poorly on humor must somehow maintain a sufficiently high romantic evaluation to have entered the sample.

text.text: Conditioning on that selection event implies that other causal parents of romantic evaluation, such as perceived intelligence, must compensate.
The result is a spurious covariance between humor and intelligence within the selected sample, even if none exists in the broader population.

In other words, approaching intertrait confounding alone would close only two of three backdoor paths: one between ideal humor preference and perceived partner humor and a second between both trait ratings of perceived partner humor and intelligence.
The backdoor path between ideal humor preference and perceived partner humor is a distinct spurious connection based on collider restriction bias as described above.
Finally, Panel B in Figure 2 depicts the structure of the level metric analytically, introducing an explicit 'Interactions' node.
text.formatted: Finally, Panel B in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref> depicts the structure of the level metric analytically, introducing an explicit 'Interactions' node.

text.text: Ideal preferences and partner attributes jointly give rise to interaction effects; the product terms entered in each (trait-by-trait) regression.
These interactions, along with both main effects, cause romantic evaluation.
Unmeasured confounders U and individual differences remain as background variables, omitted for visibility.

The dashed bidirectional arrow between ideal preferences and partner attributes is a simplified depiction which carries the same dual interpretation as in Panel A: part of the spurious covariance arises from shared background causes, and part is induced by collider conditioning on the selection event.
The level metric is designed to isolate the interaction term as the quantity of theoretical interest which indicates idiosyncratic matching effects without normative confounding.

A positive interaction coefficient for a given trait indicates that the association between perceiving that trait in a partner and evaluating them positively is stronger for participants who place greater importance on that trait (reporting a higher ideal preference for that trait).
However, biases operating on the main effects also propagate into the interaction estimates (as they are calculated in respect to corresponding main effects).
In a trait-by-trait model, the interaction coefficient therefore absorbs variance from the open backdoor paths identified in Figure 1 and Panel A in Figure 2.
text.formatted: In a trait-by-trait model, the interaction coefficient therefore absorbs variance from the open backdoor paths identified in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> and Panel A in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>.

text.text: The interaction between a humor ideal and perceived partner humor, for instance, is estimated without controlling for any other ideal preferences or partner attributes.

As explained above, even when accounting for intertrait confounding (e.g., by multivariate regression), the spurious covariance between humor ideals and perceived partner intelligence still inflates the calculated humor-matching interaction.

As previously, the third layer is linked to the third Hypothesis (H3) as posited in the introduction and tests whether idiosyncratic preference-matching effects will cluster near zero or turn insignificant after full hierarchical multivariate adjustment.
Based on the considerations derived from the previous DAGs in Figure 1 and 2, this section comprises implications for partner preference research.

text.text: As mentioned previously, the four distinct analytical approaches utilized by Eastwick et al. (2024) are of different methodological quality and show specific confounding effects of their own.
text.formatted: As mentioned previously, the four distinct analytical approaches utilized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> are of different methodological quality and show specific confounding effects of their own.

text.text: Consequently, all four approaches are briefly addressed and evaluated in respect to potentially predict idiosyncratic partner preference-matching effects.
Only after that, the three-layer structure is applied by incorporating analysis and sample-related concerns alike.
These implications are followed by general methodological concerns as a fourth layer which require attention in the context of the Eastwick et al. (2024) study design.
text.formatted: These implications are followed by general methodological concerns as a fourth layer which require attention in the context of the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> study design.

text.text: In this way, the aim of this section is to prepare the ground for establishing methodological extensions in the next section, keeping the overall goal in mind: to provide an analytical approach to offering high(er) predictive validity for partner preferencematching.
To begin with, ideal-trait correlations and the raw pattern metric are by Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 57) themselves characterize as methodologically "very weak" and "weak" respectively.
text.formatted: To begin with, ideal-trait correlations and the raw pattern metric are by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024, p.</ref> 57) themselves characterize as methodologically "very weak" and "weak" respectively.

text.text: As indicated in Chapter 3, ideal-trait-correlations do not incorporate any evaluative measure which means that they are limited in answering questions about (idiosyncratic) matching.

The raw pattern metric as such is normatively confounded because people tend to positively evaluate their relationship (high romantic evaluation) when their (most desired) partner has positive traits, irrespective of their own ideal (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 7).
text.formatted: The raw pattern metric as such is normatively confounded because people tend to positively evaluate their relationship (high romantic evaluation) when their (most desired) partner has positive traits, irrespective of their own ideal <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 7)</ref>.

text.text: Secondly, the corrected pattern metric, despite the mean-centering procedure intended to remove normative desirability confounding, remains confounded with normative preferences in trait levels (Zhao et al., 2024, p. 19).
text.formatted: Secondly, the corrected pattern metric, despite the mean-centering procedure intended to remove normative desirability confounding, remains confounded with normative preferences in trait levels <ref type="bibr">(Zhao et al., 2024, p. 19)</ref>.

text.text: Most traits which are assessed in the study are normatively desirable and, moreover, ideals are preferably rated near the ceiling of the response scale.
Consequently, partners with normatively more desirable personalities will end up with higher corrected pattern metrics, irrespective of the mean centering procedure.

As a result, it is not surprising that the corrected pattern metric correlates with positive evaluations (Schönbrodt et al., 2018, p. 628). Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 37) themselves acknowledge this by calculating an additional normative pattern metric (NPM).
text.formatted: As a result, it is not surprising that the corrected pattern metric correlates with positive evaluations <ref type="bibr">(Schönbrodt et al., 2018, p. 628)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 37)</ref> themselves acknowledge this by calculating an additional normative pattern metric (NPM).

text.text: In this approach, the evaluative outcome is predicted by correlating the individual partner traits ratings with the sample's average ideal profile (instead of participant's unique ideals).

The reported effect sizes for the NPM (β=.37) are virtually identical to the Raw Pattern Metric (RPM) estimates, pointing towards the conclusion that explicitly distinguishable idiosyncratic fit might be absent in these calculations.
Taken together, as Edwards (1994) already observed, the corrected pattern metric remains confounded with the main effects of traits (i.e., the normative preferences).

As such, CPM, although corrected, might not actually measure 'preference-matching', but rather something like perceived 'partner quality' (i.e., normatively desirable personality), which represents a different construct and raises concerns about the construct validity assumed in this analytical approach.

In the context of NPM, Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 38) conclude themselves that "effect sizes suggest that, when participants perceived that partners had normatively 'ideal' traits, they evaluated those partners very positively, regardless of their own idiosyncratic ideal partner preferences".
text.formatted: In the context of NPM, <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 38)</ref> conclude themselves that "effect sizes suggest that, when participants perceived that partners had normatively 'ideal' traits, they evaluated those partners very positively, regardless of their own idiosyncratic ideal partner preferences".

text.text: The third implication concerns the level metric, which is the only 'strong' inference methodology left to properly predict idiosyncratic matching effects in the context of the Eastwick et al. ( 2024) study (as well as of large parts of partner preference research landscape).
text.formatted: The third implication concerns the level metric, which is the only 'strong' inference methodology left to properly predict idiosyncratic matching effects in the context of the Eastwick et al. ( <ref type="formula">2024</ref>) study (as well as of large parts of partner preference research landscape).

text.text: This metric minimizes normative confounding by controlling for ideal preference and partner trait main effects within the same analytical model.
On a conceptual level, the level metric is generally implemented trait-by-trait, evaluating each ideal-trait interaction in isolation.

While Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 8) argue that the trait-by-trait approach is crucial "when testing theories positing that ideals for specific attributes have functional outcomes", it is methodologically not well justified for approaching the matching hypothesis.
text.formatted: While <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 8)</ref> argue that the trait-by-trait approach is crucial "when testing theories positing that ideals for specific attributes have functional outcomes", it is methodologically not well justified for approaching the matching hypothesis.

text.text: Since traits are intercorrelated, a bivariate model for any single trait will potentially overestimate the matching effect for that trait with matching effects flowing through correlated traits (open backdoor path in DAG terms).

While this finding mirrors the finding in the second layer and primarily reveals the issue of intertraitconfounding, the level metric is additionally estimated within a sample conditioned on (most desired partner).

As discussed within the context of the third layer, the bivariate model will probably exacerbate the inherent collider restriction bias due to the artificially high tendency of positive partner trait as well as romantic evaluations within the restricted dataset.

The pooled histogram in Figure 3 illustrates the distributional properties of the three central rating scales: partner trait ratings, ideal preference ratings and romantic evaluations, not reported by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The pooled histogram in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref> illustrates the distributional properties of the three central rating scales: partner trait ratings, ideal preference ratings and romantic evaluations, not reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: All three distributions exhibit a highly positive skew, revealing high average response tendencies and corresponding ceiling effects.

For ideal preference ratings, the skew is largely a function of the normative desirability of the provided attributes which are almost universally valued -such as attractiveness, humor, and intelligence.
This naturally produces a clustering of responses at the upper end of the scale.

For partner trait ratings and romantic evaluations, the ceiling effect is more consequential and reflects the selective nature of the sample: participants rated only a (most desired) partner whom they had deliberately chosen, meaning that partners who were perceived as clearly undesirable were largely excluded from the outset.
The degree of this truncation is substantial: 39.9% of partners received a romantic evaluation score of 10 or higher out of 11, to name just one example.
This indicates that the majority of evaluations occupy only the uppermost range of the scale.

The small but visible concentration of ratings at the lower end of the partner trait and ideal preference distributions is attributable to the four negatively worded Big Five items included to assess Agreeableness, Emotional Stability, Extraversion, and Conscientiousness (e.g., critical, quarrelsome; or anxious, easily upset; Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 13).

text.text: Ceiling effects in partner trait ratings and romantic evaluations reflect the selective composition of the (most desired) partner sample.

Moreover, the level metric relied exclusively on multilevel models without including further demographics or individual-difference measures as control covariates as indicated in the first layer and captured by the first hypothesis H1.
As the DAG in Figures 1 suggests, results are potentially confounded with these further covariates (additionally to normative desirability confounding and mediating effects between different traits).

While some important individual-difference variables have not been measured, such as subjective well-being at the time of study participation, others have only been measured but not utilized in the primary analysis.

Therefore, as specified in Section 5.2, scales for individualism/collectivism, relational mobility and further individual different measures would need to be incorporated in the regression analysis to determine whether they offer predictive validity over and above main effects and interactions.
The following implications refer to study-design related issues as a fourth layer which have not been covered in the previously introduced three-layer structure.
Study design related concerns, however, influence the four analytical approaches of partner preference-matching alike.

To start with, all partner trait ratings are reported by the same participant who also provides the romantic evaluation outcome. Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48) themselves show awareness of this concern, noting that "the participants' partners did not actually take part in this study, and effect sizes will likely decline across the board if the partner's (rather than the participant's) reports of the partner's traits are used instead" (see Hromatko et al., 2015).
text.formatted: To start with, all partner trait ratings are reported by the same participant who also provides the romantic evaluation outcome. <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 48)</ref> themselves show awareness of this concern, noting that "the participants' partners did not actually take part in this study, and effect sizes will likely decline across the board if the partner's (rather than the participant's) reports of the partner's traits are used instead" (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hromatko et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Research on relationship cognition demonstrates that global romantic satisfaction strongly motivates individuals to idealize their partners and perceive them in ways that confirm their pre-existing standards (Murray et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Research on relationship cognition demonstrates that global romantic satisfaction strongly motivates individuals to idealize their partners and perceive them in ways that confirm their pre-existing standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Murray et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: As indicated in the previous section, additional biases based on halo effects (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977) may thus further influence the reported associations.
text.formatted: As indicated in the previous section, additional biases based on halo effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Nisbett & Wilson, 1977)</ref> may thus further influence the reported associations.

text.text: This adds additional 'noise' to the dataset which is distinct from distortion due to conditioning on the collider of relationship status, however based on the same selection restriction of (most desired) partners.

Moreover, the romantic evaluation occurs at the same time as the evaluation of traits and ideals, often only after relationship formation has already occurred (or the most desired partner is already imagined).
This cross-sectional methodology raises the question in which way the study design is 'predictive' in the first place.

When taking a closer look, the study might investigate rather into causal inference. Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 16) themselves consider a reverse causality aspect, which is formally known as 'relationship formation hypothesis', by compiling a supplementary longitudinal sample.

(2024, p. 16</ref>) themselves consider a reverse causality aspect, which is formally known as 'relationship formation hypothesis', by compiling a supplementary longitudinal sample.

text.text: This study design addresses the issue that people may a posteriori adjust their assessment of corresponding partner traits to (better) match their ideals (Gerlach et al., 2019; Neff & Karney, 2003).
text.formatted: This study design addresses the issue that people may a posteriori adjust their assessment of corresponding partner traits to (better) match their ideals <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gerlach et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Neff & Karney, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: To test the hypothesis, participants first reported their partner ideals while they were single.
After entering a new romantic relationship several months later, they completed follow-up measures concerning their current romantic partner (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 10).
text.formatted: After entering a new romantic relationship several months later, they completed follow-up measures concerning their current romantic partner <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 10)</ref>.

text.text: They conclude that "[e]stimates for the steadily partnered and newly partnered sample were similar, suggesting that both sets of participants maintained their ideals over the intervening months and drew from them when evaluating their partners, regardless of whether or not they were dating that partner when they reported their ideals at time 1" (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 30).
text.formatted: They conclude that "[e]stimates for the steadily partnered and newly partnered sample were similar, suggesting that both sets of participants maintained their ideals over the intervening months and drew from them when evaluating their partners, regardless of whether or not they were dating that partner when they reported their ideals at time 1" <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 30)</ref>.

text.text: In a similar study design, Gerlach et al. (2019, p. 1) come to a slightly different conclusion, observing that "participants adjusted their preferences downward when partners fell short of initial preferences, but showed no consistent adjustment when partners exceeded them".

(2019, p. 1)</ref> come to a slightly different conclusion, observing that "participants adjusted their preferences downward when partners fell short of initial preferences, but showed no consistent adjustment when partners exceeded them".

text.text: Crucially, steady single participants in the Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 30-31) longitudinal sample showed (insignificant) corrected pattern and level metric effects near zero.
text.formatted: Crucially, steady single participants in the <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 30-31)</ref> longitudinal sample showed (insignificant) corrected pattern and level metric effects near zero.

text.text: This finding might be interpreted as supporting the presence of collider restriction bias.
If the preference-matching hypothesis holds true, it should work for everyone.
A match should predict high attraction, and a mismatch should predict low attraction, even if the interaction does not result in relationship formation.

Without conditioning on the collider of relationship formation, and most desired partner respectively, the originally observed association between preference-matching and evaluative outcomes vanishes.

While alternative explanations remain plausible, this finding might as well suggest that the predictive validity of preference matching in this particular study design may be a statistical artifact of selection.
A further study design-related implication refers to the romantic evaluation composite used by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: A further study design-related implication refers to the romantic evaluation composite used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises six items administered identically across all four nominated targetsincluding the three preferred-gender peers.
A closer inspection of the item wording, however, reveals a fundamental asymmetry between the two target types.

While items such as "I am romantically interested in [target]" and "[target] is the only person I want to be romantically involved with" are reasonably applicable to both partners and peers, several items are particularly anchored in established relational intimacy.
text.formatted: While items such as "I am romantically interested in <ref type="bibr">[target]" and "[target]</ref> is the only person I want to be romantically involved with" are reasonably applicable to both partners and peers, several items are particularly anchored in established relational intimacy.

text.text: Consequently, their application to mere acquaintances or strangers is limited.

Specifically, "[target] is the first person that I would turn to if I had a problem" and "if I achieved something good, [target] is the person that I would tell first" presuppose a degree of emotional closeness and trust that is, by definition, characteristic of formed relationships rather than the kind of newly encountered or casually known individuals who typify the peer targets.
This further constitutes the structural presence of collider restriction bias.

The romantic evaluation composite thus conflates genuine preference-matching with the relational consequences of having already chosen, rendering direct comparisons between (most desired) partners and peers problematic.
To summarize, the raised concerns can be classified as analysis-related, sample-related and study design-related implications.

The first category contains confounding by measured background variables (layer one, H1), intertrait confounding among the 35 trait ideals and partner ratings (layer two, H2) and subsequent mitigation of collider restriction bias (layer three, H3).
These concerns can potentially be solved by adapting the analytical approach.
Sample-related implications primarily refer to the remaining collider restriction bias arising from conditioning on (most desired) partners which is not targetable through analytical means.
The most direct remedy available is to apply the same model to the three unselected peer targets collected but not analyzed by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The most direct remedy available is to apply the same model to the three unselected peer targets collected but not analyzed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: As addressed in the Discussion in Chapter 7, this could further restore the excluded variation and allow a direct empirical test of whether preference-matching estimates change meaningfully outside the restricted sample.
The last category is bound to the study design used by Eastwick et al. (2024) as well as by many others within the research field of partner preference research.
text.formatted: The last category is bound to the study design used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> as well as by many others within the research field of partner preference research.

text.text: Design-related implications comprise unmeasured covariates, reverse causality aspects and halo effects, as well as the potentially skewed romantic evaluation composite.
These are inherent limitations of the research paradigm rather than of any particular analytical choice.
Corresponding biases can only be targeted by changing the design approach accordingly.
As demonstrated in the previous sections, several structurally distinct sources of bias have been identified in the partner preference research design as applied by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: As demonstrated in the previous sections, several structurally distinct sources of bias have been identified in the partner preference research design as applied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: The easiest way forward is to rule out ITC, RPM and CPM approaches for the reasons stated above and focus on the level metric as the 'gold standard' of partner preference matching effects.

When doing so, the first step of methodological improvement concerns the analysis-related implications, as they serve as necessary prerequisites for properly estimating partner preference-matching effect.
These analysis-related implications set the stage for methodological extension introduced in this section.
In addition, samplerelated concerns are briefly introduced to prepare for future research.
The first layer implicates to address confounding by measured covariates.

If these backdoor paths are left open, associations between ideal preferences, partner traits and romantic evaluation remain confounded by variables that have nothing to do with the actual matching effect itself.
The first step of the methodological strategy of this paper is thus to close these paths by including all measured confounders simultaneously in the regression model.
This is the logic of the backdoor criterion introduced in Section 2.1 (Pearl, 1993; 2000, p. 79).
text.formatted: This is the logic of the backdoor criterion introduced in Section 2.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Pearl, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2000, p. 79)</ref>.

text.text: Including demographics and individual-difference variables as covariates satisfies this criterion for the measured portion of potential confounders.
This does not resolve the unmeasured component, but it narrows the set of plausible alternative explanations, potentially reducing unsystematic 'noise'.

Moreover, following Elwert's (2013, pp. 256-257) and Shpitser et al.'s (2010, p. 530) formalization of the adjustment criterion, conditioning on variables that are ancestors of the collider variable can partially mitigate collider restriction bias, provided those variables have been measured (see also Hernán et al., 2004, pp. 620-621).
text.formatted: Moreover, following <ref type="bibr">Elwert's (2013, pp. 256-257)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Shpitser et al.'s (2010, p. 530)</ref> formalization of the adjustment criterion, conditioning on variables that are ancestors of the collider variable can partially mitigate collider restriction bias, provided those variables have been measured (see also <ref type="bibr">Hernán et al., 2004, pp. 620-621)</ref>.

text.text: The part of bias which can be mitigated is highly dependent on the degree of variance which is provided by the model.

Full recovery of collider restriction bias would theoretically occur at a coefficient of determination of R² = 1, which would mean that all unmeasured confounders would have been measured and incorporated into the analysis.

To, at least partly, account for this confounding effect, the presented regression model includes three demographic and seven individual-difference predictors that were included in the Eastwick et al. (2024) survey.
text.formatted: To, at least partly, account for this confounding effect, the presented regression model includes three demographic and seven individual-difference predictors that were included in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> survey.

text.text: Among demographics, participant age was included as a continuous variable, and both sex (coded as man as reference category, woman, or other) and sexual orientation (coded as heterosexual as reference category, bisexual, gay, lesbian, or other) were included as categorical factors.
Relationship status and length are intentionally excluded from regression modelling as they represent potential collider variables.

Among individual-difference measures, relational mobility was assessed with the 12-item scale developed by Thomson et al. (2018), capturing the perceived availability of new relationship partners and the ease of ending existing ones in a given social environment.

(2018)</ref>, capturing the perceived availability of new relationship partners and the ease of ending existing ones in a given social environment.

text.text: Individualism and collectivism were each measured at two levels using the 16-item scale by Triandis and Gelfand (1998).

text.text: Equality-based interdependence (horizontal) and hierarchy-based orientations (vertical) are differentiated across both individualist and collectivist dimensions, yielding four subscale scores in total.
Cultural tightness-looseness, referring to the strength of social norms and the tolerance of deviance within a given society, was assessed with the scale established by Gelfand et al. (2011).

text.text: All continuous individualdifference variables were entered as standardized scores to facilitate comparability of regression coefficients across predictors of differing scales.

The second layer is covered by particularly addressing intertrait confounding in the extended regression model as within-cluster associations are potentially confounded apart from collider-variableinduced dependence.
As discussed, in the trait-by-trait level metric of Eastwick et al. (2024), each regression model includes only a single ideal preference and a single partner attribute.
text.formatted: As discussed, in the trait-by-trait level metric of <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>, each regression model includes only a single ideal preference and a single partner attribute.

text.text: Every other trait in the respective cluster is therefore omitted, leaving its confounding contribution open.
The estimated interaction coefficient absorbs variance from all these open paths, inflating the apparent preferencematching effect for that trait.

To account for intertrait confounding, the regression model in this thesis closes these backdoor paths by entering all 35 ideal preferences and all 35 partner attributes as simultaneous main effects within a single model.
Each interaction coefficient can then finally be interpreted as the (analytically) unique preference-matching effect for that trait, net of all other ideal preferences and partner attributes.

As including all 35 ideal preferences and all 35 partner attributes as simultaneous main effects blocks many of these backdoor paths, it likely yields more conservative and interpretable interaction estimates.

In the same logic that was outlined in the previous sections via layer three, this methodological step additionally helps to mitigate collider restriction bias in a way that ideal and partner trait ratings are separately controlled as distinct ancestors of the collider variable of relationship status alongside demographics and individual differences.
In this sense, the hierarchical multivariate extension is the primary methodological contribution of the present study.
The predictor block of interaction effects as part of Model 4 is consequently labelled corrected level metric (CLM).
The third layer additionally implies to deal with the remaining collider restriction bias which is left after analytical adaptations of the first two layers.
Though no focus of this thesis, collider restriction bias is no property of which variables are included in the model.
It is, after all, a property of which observations are included in the sample.
Every participant in the dataset has already passed through a high-romantic-evaluation 'selection event'.
The highly skewed distributions presented in Section 4.1 reflect the structural fact that the collider has been conditioned on before any analysis begins.
Statistical adjustment can mitigate but not undo this structural flaw nor reconstitute large parts of the variation that was excluded at the point of sampling.
The preference-matching effect estimated within this sample is therefore, irrespective of properly applied regression analysis, not the population preference-matching effect.
It is the preference-matching effect among people who are already in or pursuing a positively evaluated relationship.
Therefore, the most robust methodological solution to address the issue of collider restriction bias, apart from confounding issues, is to utilize a less conditional sample.
Notably, this approach is possible due to the 'unselected' peer targets which have been collected but not used by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Notably, this approach is possible due to the 'unselected' peer targets which have been collected but not used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: To predict partner preference matching effects, however, the first two layers of the extended methodological approach are essential prerequisites for the third layer.
Therefore, the thesis focuses on testing the multivariate regression model on the same dataset used by Eastwick et al. (2024).

The resulting interaction coefficients should therefore be understood as more conservative, less biased estimates than those from the trait-by-trait approach, not as bias-free estimates of the true population parameter.

text.text: The following chapter specifies the method of the hierarchical extension in detail, from the baseline replication to the demographic model through to the full preference-matching interaction model.
Based on previous considerations, the present study constituted a secondary analysis of the dataset collected by Eastwick et al. (2024) as described in Chapter 3.

text.text: The analysis proceeded in two steps.

The first step consisted of a full replication of the level metric analyses reported by Eastwick et al. (2024), serving as a validation of the analytical framework prior to the proposed methodological extension.

text.text: Secondly, the hierarchical multivariate regression model was developed to address the three analysisrelated structurally distinct sources of bias identified in the methodological framework in Chapter 3.
Primarily, the analysis addressed confounding by measured background variables and intertrait confounding among the 35 trait ratings.
As described in Section 4.2 the analysis thereby potentially mitigated collider restriction bias by controlling for corresponding ancestors of the collider variable.
All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2026).

Annotated R code for data processing, level metric replication, hierarchical regression analysis as well as model comparison is provided in Appendix A. text.text: To assess whether this algorithmic difference introduced any meaningful discrepancy, two alternative optimizers were applied to two exemplary attributes, intelligence and religiosity, and the resulting fixed and varying effect estimates were compared directly.

Differences between the two optimizers were negligible, ranging from the fifth to the seventh decimal place depending on the attribute, providing sufficient justification for the use of bobyqa throughout all subsequent analyses.

The replication was successful, recovering the pattern of results reported in the original study, including the substantially larger level metric effect for religiosity (β = .13) relative to intelligence (β = .03), consistent with Eastwick et al.

text.text: To account for all three layers as presented in Section 4.2, the methodological extension was implemented as a hierarchical multilevel model built across four steps (Models 1-4).
In each step one predictor block was added to the preceding model.
Model 1 included only the demographic and individual-difference covariates alongside a varying intercept, establishing the baseline variance explained by background characteristics.
Model 2 extended Model 1 by adding the standardized main effects of all 35 partner attributes simultaneously.

In addition to the remaining varying intercept in Model 1, 35 varying slopes for each partner attribute were added to Model 2 in correspondence to the analytical approach of Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 22).
text.formatted: In addition to the remaining varying intercept in Model 1, 35 varying slopes for each partner attribute were added to Model 2 in correspondence to the analytical approach of <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 22)</ref>.

text.text: Model 3 further added the standardized main effects of all 35 ideal preferences.
Model 4 introduced all 35 Ideal × PartnerAttribute product terms as the preference-matching estimates of primary theoretical interest.
Models 3 and 4 retained the same varying effects structure as Model 2.

Because simultaneously estimating 35 varying slopes across k = 60 Level-2 units risks over-parameterization, the varying effects covariance matrix was specified as diagonal, constraining off-diagonal covariances to zero.
In other words, samples are assumed to vary independently of one another in terms of intercept and slopes.
This assumption is justified by the absence of a strong a priori theory regarding the specific co-variation of the 35 traits as well as by technical feasibility.

Following this approach, the parameter space from over 600 covariance terms was reduced to 36 variance components while retaining the theoretically motivated heterogeneity of partner attribute slopes across cultural samples as proposed by Eastwick et al. (2024).

Some predictors of demographics and individual difference scales reached comparatively high effects.

Age emerged as the strongest and most consistent effect across all models (Model 4: β = .12***), indicating that older participants evaluate their partners more positively independent of which partner attributes are perceived.
Women reported higher romantic evaluation than men after controlling for all other predictors (Model 4: β = .09***), a tendency that is stable across Models 1 through 4.

The most pronounced demographic effect was observed for participants identifying as "other" in sexual orientation (N = 361), who reported substantially lower romantic evaluation than self-reported hetero-, homo-and bisexual participants across all model specifications (Model 4: β = -.18***).

Among individualdifference predictors, vertical collectivism was the only scale that remains positively significant across all four models (β = .04***), suggesting that participants who valued hierarchy-based group cohesion evaluated their partners more favorably.

Preference-matching interaction effects
The preference-matching interaction terms are displayed in Panel 3 of Figure 4 and constitute the primary theoretical focus of the present thesis.

text.text: In the Eastwick et al. (2024) replication, interaction coefficients were uniformly positive, ranging from β = .00 to β = .13, with the large majority statistically significant.
In Model 4, interaction coefficients were once again systematically attenuated.
Point estimates clustered between β = -.02 and β = .03, with the majority being non-significant.
Only the interactions for A good lover (β = .02***), Humorous (β = .03***) and Religious (β = .03***) remained significant to the level of p < .001.
text.formatted: Only the interactions for A good lover (β = .02***), Humorous (β = .03***) and Religious (β = .03***) remained significant to the level of p < .001.

text.text: Across both models, the Religiosity interaction was the most robust and the most attenuated in absolute terms (Eastwick et al. replication: β = .13; Model 4: β = .03).
This pattern is consistent with the observation that religiosity is the trait in the set with the greatest idiosyncratic variance.

Unlike normatively desirable attributes for which virtually all participants reported high ideals, religiosity preferences vary substantially across participants, preserving the within-person variance necessary to detect genuine moderation.

The attenuation of this interaction from .13 to .03 between the two models is itself illustrative of the potential inflation produced by uncontrolled confounding in the trait-by-trait approach, even for highly varying attributes.
Likelihood ratio tests confirmed that each successive predictor block improved model fit significantly.

The addition of 35 partner attribute main effects in Model 2 produced by far the largest improvement over the demographic baseline of Model 1, Δχ²(70) = 5790.73, p < .001, indicating that perceived partner characteristics account for substantial variance in romantic evaluation over and above participant-level covariates.

text.text: The further inclusion of 35 ideal preference main effects in Model 3 yielded a statistically significant but considerably smaller improvement, Δχ²(35) = 132.32, p < .001.

text.text: Most critically, the addition of the 35 Idealₖ × PartnerAttributeₖ interaction terms in Model 4 again improved fit over Model 3, Δχ²(35) = 88.34, p < .001, providing evidence that preference-matching effects account for some variance in romantic evaluation net of all main effects.

text.text: However, information criteria AIC (Akaike information criterion) and BIC (Bayesian information criterion) revealed a diverging picture.
AIC decreased consistently across all four models, indicating that each successive predictor block improved the tradeoff between fit and parsimony accordingly.
The reduction from Model 1 to Model 2 was by far the largest (ΔAIC = -5650), with only modest further reductions when ideal preferences (ΔAIC = -63) and interactions (ΔAIC = -18) were added.

Though BIC decreased substantially from Model 1 to Model 2 (ΔBIC = -5145), it slightly increased when ideal preferences were added in Model 3 (ΔBIC = +190) and again when interactions were added in Model 4 (ΔBIC = +234).

From a BIC perspective, which applies a more stringent penalty for model complexity, neither ideal preferences nor preference-matching interactions improve the model sufficiently to offset the 'cost' of 35 additional parameters each.
Variance decomposition as reported in the four last rows of Table 1 logically supported likelihood ratio test results.
