text.text: The following sections contextualize the results presented in Chapter 6.

The central findings are organized around the five analytical sections of the previous chapter, each corresponding to a specific layer of the methodological framework and an associated hypothesis (H1-H3).
Subsequently, broader theoretical and methodological implications are derived from the central findings before directions for future research are presented.
H1, in correspondence with layer 1 implications, receives mixed support.

Effect sizes for some demographic predictors and individual-difference scales were relatively high, especially in comparison to the attenuated effect sizes of both main effects (partner trait and ideal preference ratings) as well as interaction effects (idiosyncratic share of actual matching effects).

This finding is especially notable as Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 44) stated that preregistered tests of individual differences showed "no interpretable pattern" and that no functional outcomes could be derived from them.
text.formatted: This finding is especially notable as <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 44)</ref> stated that preregistered tests of individual differences showed "no interpretable pattern" and that no functional outcomes could be derived from them.

text.text: However, their collective contribution to preference-matching estimates is relatively marginal in terms of explained variance represented by a small coefficient of determination in Model 1 (R² ).

Moreover, the two sign reversals of relational mobility and horizontal collectivism in Model 2 indicate that individual-difference effects on romantic evaluation are substantially mediated by perceived partner attributes rather than operating independently.
This observation is further supported, when Model 4 was stripped off any background characteristics.
The resulting loss of variance was negligible (ΔR²fixed = .009).
After all, the combination of relatively high effects and marginal variance of individual preferences might partly be explained by the specific configuration of the sample.

To name just one example, many participants were recruited in a university context resulting in a relatively low standard deviation and mean of participants age (M = 28.5, SD = 11.7 years) compared to true population parameters.
Little variance in age consequently results in a relatively small potential for age to explain variance in romantic evaluations. replication model.
Changes in unique ideal preference effects, however, were highly ambiguous.
This additional noteworthy pattern shows that across both models, a substantial number of ideal preference coefficients were positive, many of them normatively highly desirable.

The pattern theoretically indicates that participants who place greater importance on a given trait also evaluate their partner more positively, independently of how highly they actually rate their partner on that trait.
This pattern is considerably more pronounced in the Eastwick et al. (2024) replication, but it persists in Model 4 as well.
text.formatted: This pattern is considerably more pronounced in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> replication, but it persists in Model 4 as well.

text.text: Under the preference-matching hypothesis, this direction of effect is difficult to justify: if a participant values a trait highly and their partner falls short of that standard, the ideal should function as a critical benchmark, producing lower rather than higher romantic evaluation.

A positive main effect of the ideal may reflect a general positivity artifact: participants who rate any given trait as highly important may also tend to perceive their (most desired) partner as highly desirable overall, producing a spurious positive association between ideal ratings and romantic evaluation that has little to do with idiosyncratic preference structure.
Religiosity constitutes an instructive counterexample.
Both the Eastwick et al.
(2024) replication and Model 4 report a negative ideal preference main effect for religiosity.
It means that participants who place greater importance on religiosity in a partner evaluate their (most desired) partner less positively, net of their partner's religiosity rating.

This is precisely the direction which is expected in the context of the ideal preference logic: religiosity is one of the few attributes in the set for which individual preferences vary substantially rather than clustering near the ceiling of the ideal scale, making it possible for high ideals to exert downward pressure on romantic evaluation.
This theoretically expected negative effect emerges for religiosity, but not for most normatively desirable traits which points, at least in parts, toward a study design-related concern.

The ceiling effects documented in Figure 3, combined with the restriction to (most desired) partners, may suppress the critical benchmark function of ideals for attributes that are near-universally valued.
text.formatted: The ceiling effects documented in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>, combined with the restriction to (most desired) partners, may suppress the critical benchmark function of ideals for attributes that are near-universally valued.

text.text: Only traits with genuine crossparticipant variance, such as religiosity, are consequently capable of producing the expected pattern.
Whether this reflects a structural limitation of the sample, the measurement instrument, or both warrants careful consideration in future research designs.
H3 is, in alignment with the third layer, supported by the near-zero effect sizes of interactions.
All 35 traits in Model 4 clustered between β = -.02 and β = .03 and, once again, were substantially attenuated.
In this sense H2 receives additional support.
With 95% confidence intervals broadly overlapping zero in Figure 4, few of them were significant.
text.formatted: With 95% confidence intervals broadly overlapping zero in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>, few of them were significant.

text.text: After all, only three idiosyncratic matching effect sizes remained significant at the level of p < .001 in Model 4.
text.formatted: After all, only three idiosyncratic matching effect sizes remained significant at the level of p < .001 in Model 4.

text.text: This finding reflects a general observation that once all 35 attributes are incorporated via the hierarchical regression analysis, a large majority of attributes which had been significant in the trait-by-trait approach, turned insignificant across all predictor blocks.

As no multiple comparison correction was applied, it is worth noting that a Holm-Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979) applied to the 35 interaction terms yields a corrected threshold of α = .05/35 = .00143, below which all three significant effects remain.
text.formatted: As no multiple comparison correction was applied, it is worth noting that a Holm-Bonferroni correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Holm, 1979</ref>) applied to the 35 interaction terms yields a corrected threshold of α = .05/35 = .00143, below which all three significant effects remain.

text.text: A stricter correction across all fixed-effect model terms would, however, likely render these effects non-significant as well, further underscoring the overall fragility of the preference-matching signal.
Additional support for H3 is provided by the stark attenuation of ideal preferences.
Because the partner attribute rating is held constant in the same model, the ideal coefficient potentially captures the discrepancy between what the participant wants and what the partner provides.
For any fixed level of perceived partner quality on a given trait, a higher ideal means a larger unmet gap between standard and reality.
The mostly insignificant near-zero effects observed in Model 4 thus indicate that ideals do apparently not function as critical standards against which partners are evaluated.

Consequently, H3 receives strong empirical support by utilizing the corrected level metric: even after full multivariate adjustment, idiosyncratic preference-matching effects are very small and statistically fragile.
The near-zero ideal preference matching effects (interactions) in Model 4 constitute one of the clearest findings of the present study (H3).

Once general partner quality, approximated by the simultaneous inclusion of all 35 partner attribute ratings, is accounted for, stated ideal preferences and interactions carry extremely low residual predictive value for romantic evaluation.

Adding all 35 partner attribute main effects in Model 2 yielded to an increase in variance explained (ΔR²fixed) of more than 70 times higher than the subsequent addition of ideal preferences in Model 3 and more than 105 times higher than the final addition of interactions in Model 4.
The BIC penalty for adding ideal preferences in Model 3 and interactions in Model 4 underscores that neither block improves model fit sufficiently to justify the additional 35 parameters each.
In this sense, partner trait ratings provide by far the largest share of variance to explain romantic evaluation.

The likelihood ratio test, however, formally confirmed that the 35 interactions collectively improved model fit over Model 3, providing formal evidence that preferencematching is not wholly absent in the utilized study design.
However so, the (uncorrected) level metric might in large parts measure perceived 'partner quality' as a different construct after all.

As stated in the introduction, these findings are consistent with (at least) two theoretical arguments: either collider bias arising from conditioning on (most desired) partners constitutes a structural property of the sample that full multivariate regression adjustment cannot correct or the study-design itself is limited to detect idiosyncratic matching effects in the first place.
The latter explanation points towards a third possible explanation: asked in the way the study design implies, people don't say (or know) what they really want after all.

Consequently, what people say they want may itself reflect normative desirability standards or social presentation rather than idiosyncratic evaluative criteria that actually guide their romantic judgments.
This finding connects directly to the distinction between stated and revealed preferences as conceptualized by Wood and Brumbaugh (2009).
text.formatted: This finding connects directly to the distinction between stated and revealed preferences as conceptualized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Wood and Brumbaugh (2009)</ref>.

text.text: Stated preferences (ideal ratings) reflect what participants say they want.
Revealed preferences (partner attributes main effects) represent what actually drives romantic evaluation, regardless of what participants report.
Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 32-34) demonstrate that these systematically diverge in ranking across many of the 35 attributes reported.

A stated preference for intelligence may reflect a normative belief about desirable partner qualities rather than an operative criterion that modulates how intelligent partners are actually evaluated.
The spread of Eastwick ideal preference effects in both directions is itself informative in this regard.
The positive effects for traits like Confident potentially reflect general partner quality leaking into the ideal coefficient in the absence of full partner attribute controls.

Taken together, the present results support the conclusion that romantic evaluation is driven primarily by who the partner is perceived to be, not by the alignment between that perception and what the evaluator claims to want.

This explanation is supported by the fact that steady single participants in the Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 30-31) longitudinal sample showed insignificant corrected pattern and level metric effects near zero (in contrast to newly or steadily partnered individuals).
text.formatted: This explanation is supported by the fact that steady single participants in the <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 30-31</ref>) longitudinal sample showed insignificant corrected pattern and level metric effects near zero (in contrast to newly or steadily partnered individuals).

text.text: If the preference-matching hypothesis would properly be addressed by the current research design, it should work for everyone.

The strong compression of partner attribute main effects in Model 4 is a further notable result of the present study, and its structural explanation is transparent within the methodological framework.
In the trait-by-trait approach, each partner attribute coefficient absorbs the variance it shares with all correlated traits omitted from the model.
Entering all 35 attributes simultaneously in Model 4 yielded clearly attenuated effects net of their shared (or mediated) covariance.
The substantial intercorrelation among partner attribute ratings reflects potential halo effects, shared normative desirability covariance and unknown mediating structure among the 35 attributes.
After all, the reduction in apparent predictive weight is both expected and theoretically interpretable as direct evidence of Layer 2 intertrait confounding.

The simultaneous entry of measured ancestors of the collider variable additionally achieves partial mitigation of Layer 3 collider restriction bias, meaning the two mechanisms operate simultaneously and cannot be fully separated within the present design.

However, as additional variance of measured background characteristics is extremely low, the mitigating effect on collider restriction bias apart from intertrait confounding is likely to be relatively small in the analytical model.

As discussed in the next section, this finding reflects the limitations of analysis-related methodological extensions and leads to the necessity to utilize another sample in order to reconstitute the variance lost by condition on (most) desired partner.
Importantly, sign reversals as well as small effect sizes in Model 4 carry a ceteris paribus interpretation that requires attention for all predictor blocks.
A negative and negligible partner trait main effect for Sporty and athletic for instance, does not mean that athletic partners are evaluated less positively in general.
The Eastwick et al. (2024) trait-by-trait replication shows the opposite.
text.formatted: The <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> trait-by-trait replication shows the opposite.

text.text: It means that conditional on all other 35 partner attributes being held constant, perceived athleticism contributes a small negative increment to romantic evaluation.
This finding is consistent with an intertrait mediation structure and risks overcontrol bias as mentioned in Chapter 2 (see Rohrer, 2018, p. 38; Rohrer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with an intertrait mediation structure and risks overcontrol bias as mentioned in Chapter 2 (see <ref type="bibr">Rohrer, 2018, p. 38;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Rohrer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The positive marginal effect of athletic, for instance, might flow through correlated appearancerelated traits such as attractive and nice body.
Equally and additionally possible is the explanation that shared confounding background variance is removed by the multivariate approach, such as by normative desirability standards.
The present design cannot differentiate between these explanations.

The practical implication, however, is that near-zero and negative coefficients in Model 4 should not be interpreted as evidence that a specific trait is irrelevant to romantic evaluation, but that its effect is not uniquely distinguishable once the full trait space is controlled.
This ceteris paribus constraint equally applies to the interaction terms, where near-zero estimates may reflect fully mediated matching effects rather than genuine absence.
Furthermore, the simultaneous inclusion of 35 traits, 35 ideals, and their 35 respective interaction terms in a single multivariate model theoretically raises concerns regarding multicollinearity.

The empirical inspection of the standard errors, however, shows the average standard errors for the level metric interactions in the comprehensive multivariate model were lower or equal than those obtained from the isolated, trait-by-trait replication.
While multicollinearity typically inflates standard errors, this observed shrinkage indicates a substantial reduction in the model's residual variance.

Consequently, the saturated multivariate model does not 'suffer' from coefficient instability; rather, it yields slightly more robust estimates by successfully isolating the unique predictive validity of each preference-matching interaction.

The observed pattern is consistent with a growing body of literature and underscores the analytic advantage of simultaneous estimation. (Feng et al., 2019; Graham, 2003; Gregorich et al., 2021; Morrissey & Ruxton, 2018; O'Brien, 2007; Vanhove, 2021).
text.formatted: The observed pattern is consistent with a growing body of literature and underscores the analytic advantage of simultaneous estimation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Feng et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Graham, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Gregorich et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Morrissey & Ruxton, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">O'Brien, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vanhove, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Directions for future research Several structurally distinct issues remain unresolved by the present analysis and define the most productive directions for subsequent work.
The most consequential is the residual layer 3 collider restriction bias.
The analysis-related multivariate adjustment addresses Layers 1 and 2 but cannot properly reconstitute the sample-related variation excluded by restricting the analysis to (most desired) partners.
The highly positively skewed distributions documented in Figure 3, with 39.9% of partners receiving romantic evaluation scores of 10 or higher out of 11, reflect this structural truncation.
text.formatted: The highly positively skewed distributions documented in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>, with 39.9% of partners receiving romantic evaluation scores of 10 or higher out of 11, reflect this structural truncation.

text.text: Ceiling effects of this magnitude risk sample-dependent influence on effect sizes whereby high romantic evaluation is given by construction.
The most apparent available remedy is to apply the same hierarchical multivariate model to the three unselected peer targets collected but not analyzed by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The most apparent available remedy is to apply the same hierarchical multivariate model to the three unselected peer targets collected but not analyzed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Inclusion of these targets likely reconstitutes parts of the excluded variation by drawing from a more representative evaluation range of romantic evaluation.
Thereby, comparison of both samples with the corrected level metric provides a direct empirical test of whether preferencematching interactions are further distorted by collider restriction bias.

In this sense, the sample comparison provides a deeper understanding of the research question which guided this thesis: "To what extent does collider bias distort the predictive validity of ideal partner preferences?".
Second, the six-item romantic evaluation composite includes items presupposing relational intimacy as demonstrated in Section 4.1.
Applying this specific scale across selected and unselected targets risks introducing asymmetric measurement error that confounds comparisons across target types.
A revised composite calibrated to evaluative function across both target types, or alternatively, separate composite specifications, would strengthen future extension to the unselected peer sample.
A third unresolved issue is the mediation problem introduced by simultaneous entry of all 35 partner attributes.
Some intertrait correlations treated as confounding in Model 4 are plausibly causal (or predictive respectively).
The attribute attractive, for instance, may partly cause perceptions of sporty and athletic or nice body; ambitious may causally precede a perceived successful and so on.
Susceptible to overcontrol bias, near-zero coefficients in Model 4 may reflect full mediation rather than genuine zero effects as discussed previously.

Addressing this formally requires a prespecified causal ordering among the 35 traits -a theoretically demanding step that would require dedicated theoretical and empirical work beyond the present scope.
Finally, design-related implications as introduced in Section 4.1 point towards additional directions for future research.

The collection of unmeasured covariates such as subjective well-being at the time of participation (or transsituational), reverse causality aspects and halo effects might additionally be addressed to reduce apparent confounding.

Many more potential sources of biased estimation which have not explicitly been discussed would require further attention such as method variance, measurement error (Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016), rater effects, and IKEA effects (Norton et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Many more potential sources of biased estimation which have not explicitly been discussed would require further attention such as method variance, measurement error <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Westfall & Yarkoni, 2016)</ref>, rater effects, and IKEA effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Norton et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The overall utility of these potential considerations is highly dependent on the methodological quality of the underlying research design which, after all, is in question as concluded in the next chapter.
This thesis was motivated by a structural concern that has received inadequate attention in the partner preference literature up until today.
As introduced by Eastwick & Neff (2012, p. 667) most individuals are able to readily describe the qualities they would like in an ideal romantic partner.
text.formatted: As introduced by <ref type="bibr">Eastwick & Neff (2012, p. 667</ref>) most individuals are able to readily describe the qualities they would like in an ideal romantic partner.

text.text: These descriptions often vary considerably, with some people valuing a caring and supportive partner who provides affection during difficult times, while others place greater importance on traits such as confidence and social competence.
Whether these individually stated preferences predict whom people end up with, and how positively they evaluate them, is the central question of the partner preference-matching literature.
The preference-matching hypothesis states that people evaluate romantic partners more favorably the more closely a partner's attributes match their stated ideals (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5).
text.formatted: The preference-matching hypothesis states that people evaluate romantic partners more favorably the more closely a partner's attributes match their stated ideals <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5</ref>).

text.text: If one rates intelligence as highly desirable, is one more likely to evaluate an intelligent partner positively?
Does this variation in preferences explain why people are romantically drawn to some individuals rather than others?

These questions are central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model (Fletcher et al., 1999 (Fletcher et al., , 2000;; Simpson et al., 2001) that have motivated decades of empirical investigation (Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485).
text.formatted: These questions are central to influential theoretical frameworks such as the Ideal Standards Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fletcher et al., 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fletcher et al., , 2000;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Simpson et al., 2001</ref>) that have motivated decades of empirical investigation <ref type="bibr">(Campbell & Stanton, 2014, p. 485)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this longevity, empirical support for the matching hypothesis has remained surprisingly inconsistent, and concerns about the predictive validity of the underlying research designs have been largely unaddressed (Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5; Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1).
text.formatted: Despite this longevity, empirical support for the matching hypothesis has remained surprisingly inconsistent, and concerns about the predictive validity of the underlying research designs have been largely unaddressed <ref type="bibr">(Eastwick et al., 2024, p. 5;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gerlach et al., 2019, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation for this phenomenon is introduced in Chapter 1 of this thesis: commonly utilized research designs that find support for the preference-matching hypothesis, as conducted by Eastwick et al. (2024), inherently condition their analysis on romantic partners.
text.formatted: One possible explanation for this phenomenon is introduced in Chapter 1 of this thesis: commonly utilized research designs that find support for the preference-matching hypothesis, as conducted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>, inherently condition their analysis on romantic partners.

text.text: Thereby, researcher test their hypotheses in an artificial world of high romantic evaluation, which is not representative of the true population.

As a common effect of the predictors under investigation (partner attributes as well as ideal preferences), romantic partners represent a collider variable based on the classical inverted fork structure as formalized in Chapter 2.

The following introduction of the directed acyclic graph methodology (DAG) as a framework for causal reasoning demonstrated that conditioning on a collider potentially introduces collider restriction bias (Lu et al., 2023, pp. 407-408).
text.formatted: The following introduction of the directed acyclic graph methodology (DAG) as a framework for causal reasoning demonstrated that conditioning on a collider potentially introduces collider restriction bias <ref type="bibr">(Lu et al., 2023, pp. 407-408)</ref>.

text.text: As the analysis by Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 43), which was described in Chapter 3, represents "the largest examination of ideal partner preference-matching to date", it is especially appropriate for further investigation into the ramifications of collider restriction bias in the context of partner preference research.
text.formatted: As the analysis by <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 43)</ref>, which was described in Chapter 3, represents "the largest examination of ideal partner preference-matching to date", it is especially appropriate for further investigation into the ramifications of collider restriction bias in the context of partner preference research.

text.text: Eastwick et al.
(2024, p. 13) applied a study design which deliberately included single participants into the analysis to address the issue of relationship status.

However, as Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 25, 28, 30) themselves reported multiple times, the differences of partnered participants, who rated their current romantic partner, and single participants, who rated their most desired partner, tended to be "very small".
text.formatted: However, as <ref type="bibr">Eastwick et al. (2024, pp. 25, 28, 30)</ref> themselves reported multiple times, the differences of partnered participants, who rated their current romantic partner, and single participants, who rated their most desired partner, tended to be "very small".

text.text: In the present context, this finding can be read as a hint that replacing established by most desired partners has no substantial mitigating effect on collider restriction bias.

Based on these observations, the current thesis approached the following research question: "To what extent does collider bias distort the predictive validity of ideal partner preferences in the Eastwick et al. (2024) data analysis?".
To provide potential answers, the analysis conducted by Eastwick et al. (2024) was methodologically assessed by drawing inferences from three distinct DAGs in Chapter 4.
The evaluation revealed several additional sources of bias which primarily need to be addressed to properly account for collider bias in a subsequent analysis.
Consequently, a three-layered framework with specific analytical implications for the analysis as applied by Eastwick et al. (2024) was introduced.
text.formatted: Consequently, a three-layered framework with specific analytical implications for the analysis as applied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> was introduced.

text.text: The first two layers comprise analysis-related implications.
The third layer marks the transition from analysis to sample-related concerns.
A fourth layer was additionally introduced to capture study design-related issues which cannot be accounted for in the context of this thesis.
Layer 1 concerns confounding by measured background variables.
Layer 2 indicates intertrait confounding among the 35 ideal preference and partner attribute ratings.
Layer 3 points towards collider restriction bias arising from conditioning on the most desired or established partner.
The latter represents a structural property of the sample that regression adjustment can only partially correct by controlling for causally preceding influences of the collider variable.

In response to the methodological assessment, a hierarchical multivariate extension of the level metric was developed in Chapter 5 to address Layers 1 and 2 analytically, while acknowledging that Layer 3 remains largely beyond the reach of within-sample statistical correction.
Four hypotheses guided the empirical analysis.

H0 restated the preference-matching hypothesis of Eastwick et al. (2024) as the theoretical baseline, predicting positive and significant interaction effects between partner and ideal trait ratings for the original level metric.
text.formatted: H0 restated the preference-matching hypothesis of <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> as the theoretical baseline, predicting positive and significant interaction effects between partner and ideal trait ratings for the original level metric.

text.text: The following three hypotheses were conceptualized in a way that they correspond with the three layers introduced in Chapter 4.
H1 predicted that demographic and individual-difference covariates would produce additional significant effect sizes in the full hierarchical model.
H2 predicted that simultaneous multivariate intertrait adjustment would substantially attenuate both attribute main effects and interaction coefficients.
H3 stated that even after full multivariate adjustment, preference-matching interactions would remain near zero.

As stated in the introduction, H3 is consistent with (at least) two theoretical arguments: either collider bias arising from conditioning on (most desired) partners constitutes a structural property of the sample that full multivariate regression adjustment cannot correct or the study-design itself is limited to detect idiosyncratic matching effects in the first place.
The latter explanation is based on layer four implications and points towards a third possible explanation.
Asked in the way the study design implies, people may not say, or even know, what they actually want.
To find support for the stated hypotheses, the present study pursued two interconnected goals.

The first aim was to replicate the level metric of Eastwick et al. (2024) as it was evaluated as potentially providing the strongest predictive inference amongst the four analytically distinct methods applied by Eastwick et al. (2024).
text.formatted: The first aim was to replicate the level metric of <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> as it was evaluated as potentially providing the strongest predictive inference amongst the four analytically distinct methods applied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Against this benchmark, the hierarchical multivariate regression model was developed to address the three structurally distinct sources of bias as mentioned above (Model 1 -Model 4).
The results of the full hierarchical multivariate regression model, as well as of the consequently established corrected level metric, were presented in Chapter 6.
The discussion in Chapter 7 provided the necessary contextualization of the results and subsequently reflected on implications and directions for future research.
In this sense, the present thesis reached out to examine whether the original level metric of Eastwick et al. (2024) yields valid estimates of idiosyncratic preference-matching.
text.formatted: In this sense, the present thesis reached out to examine whether the original level metric of <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> yields valid estimates of idiosyncratic preference-matching.

text.text: The findings across three analytical layers and four hypotheses converge into a methodologically properly incorporating all measured causally upstream variables (layer 1 and 2); and where the sampling design imposes a ceiling on valid inference that no statistical model can overcome (layer 3).
So far, the methodological multivariate extension developed in this thesis is not able to distinguish between the two.
Without considering a different sample to be compared via the corrected level metric, the answer cannot be provided within the utilized sample itself.
As discussed in Section 7.3, this approach is a rigorous and highly recommended possibility to provide a deeper understanding of the research question which initially guided this thesis.
Notably, the 'unselected' peer targets which have been collected but not used by Eastwick et al. (2024) provide the necessary data for future research.
text.formatted: Notably, the 'unselected' peer targets which have been collected but not used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> provide the necessary data for future research.

text.text: In this sense, the research question was only insufficiently answered in the context of this thesis.
Nevertheless, the present findings raise a fundamental challenge for H0 as conventionally conceptualized.
The preference-matching hypothesis assumes that stated ideal preferences are valid proxies for the individual preference structures that guide romantic evaluation.
The current analysisrelated results point towards the fact that the operationalization as applied by Eastwick et al. (2024) might address a different construct.
text.formatted: The current analysisrelated results point towards the fact that the operationalization as applied by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> might address a different construct.

text.text: As mostly normatively desirable partner trait ratings constitute the overwhelmingly dominant predictor block of romantic evaluation in the present sample, the uncorrected level metric might rather address the construct of perceived 'partner quality' when applied trait-by-trait.
This observation is supported by the near-zero interaction effects after all 35 attributes are controlled for.

Moreover, the systematic divergence between stated preferences (i.e., ideal ratings) and revealed preferences (i.e., partner attributes main effects) point towards the possibility that what people say they want may itself reflect normative desirability standards rather than idiosyncratic evaluative criteria guiding their romantic judgments.
The issue at hand is intensified by complementary biases which have only briefly been discussed in the context of this thesis.

Arising from the additional study-design related fourth layer, halo effects (Murray et al., 1996; Nisbett & Wilson, 1977), IKEA effects (Norton et al., 2011) and reverse causality aspects (Gerlach et al., 2019) inflate individual attribute ratings, especially when initial attraction is high.
text.formatted: Arising from the additional study-design related fourth layer, halo effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Murray et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Nisbett & Wilson, 1977)</ref>, IKEA effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Norton et al., 2011)</ref> and reverse causality aspects <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gerlach et al., 2019)</ref> inflate individual attribute ratings, especially when initial attraction is high.

text.text: As high romantic evaluations are the condition for being in the sample in the first place, the resulting 'upward pressure' on perceived partner trait ratings that follows is not deliberate misreporting; it is a structural artifact of collider conditioning.
This dynamic is an essential reason why the above-mentioned sources of bias as well as intertrait confounding are potentially exacerbated when conditioning on a sample-restricting collider.
Additionally, the cross-sectional study design raises the question in which way the study design is 'predictive' in the first place.

As demonstrated in Chapter 4, these considerations likely also apply to the other three analytically distinct approaches which have been utilized by Eastwick et al. (2024) apart from the level metric.
text.formatted: As demonstrated in Chapter 4, these considerations likely also apply to the other three analytically distinct approaches which have been utilized by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> apart from the level metric.

text.text: Note in this context that predictive validity, framed by Eastwick et al. (2024, p. 3), and valid causal inference are not necessarily the same.
text.formatted: Note in this context that predictive validity, framed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024, p.</ref> 3), and valid causal inference are not necessarily the same.

text.text: However, as causality presupposes predictivity, causal reasoning offers an adequate way of targeting aspects of predictive validity (see e.g., Kraemer et al., 1997, p. 341).
text.formatted: However, as causality presupposes predictivity, causal reasoning offers an adequate way of targeting aspects of predictive validity (see e.g., <ref type="bibr">Kraemer et al., 1997, p. 341)</ref>.

text.text: As this issue reaches far beyond the scope of this thesis, no further attempt at differentiation is made at this point.

Finally, the overall utility of sample-and study design-related adaptations as proposed in Section 7.3 highly depends on the potential of the current research design to actually test partner preferencematching effects.
The apparent dominance of normative partner desirability might at least partly reflect a consequence of study design-related measurement conditions rather than a feature of the underlying sample.
This account is substantive and points towards the construct validity of the ideal preference model itself.

Reduced to explicit single-item importance ratings with an unknown mediation structure, the 35-item conceptualization only captures a highly accessible and normatively common layer of partner preferences.

The more idiosyncratic, non-verbal, contextually embedded, or potentially irrational dimensions of actual attraction are, the less likely they are to be adequately represented by such a measurement approach.

If the present operationalization were to systematically underspecify the complexity of genuine individual preferences, preference-matching effects would be attenuated: not primarily because matching is irrelevant and less due to conditioning on the collider variable of (most desired) partners, but because the utilized instrument would lack the measurement depth required to detect it.

(2024) the following items have been reverse-scored # Affects items 26, 28, 30, 32, 34 in Table 3 (Agr1, Neu1, Ext2, Con2, Ope2) # commented out for better interpretation of BigFive traits on romantic evaluation # Reverse-score negatively-worded Big Five items (scale 1-11: reversed = 12 -original) # bfi_reverse <-c("Agr1", "Neu1", "Ext2", "Con2", "Ope2") # # for (trait in bfi_reverse) { # dat [[paste0("P1_", trait)]] <- 12 -dat[[paste0("P1_", trait)]] # dat [[paste0("Ideal_", trait)]] <- trait)]] # } traits_table3 <-c( "attract","intell","humor","consid","honest","underst", "amb","sporty","fun","sensitive","goodlove","nicebod", "conf","sexy","finsec","support","dress","goodlis","loyal", "success","advent","job","relig","patient", "Ext1","Agr1","Con1","Neu1","Ope1", "Ext2","Agr2","Con2","Neu2","Ope2","smgood" ) labels_table3 <-c( "Attractive","Intelligent","Humorous","Considerate","Honest", "Understanding","Ambitious","Sporty and athletic","Fun","Sensitive", "A good lover","Nice body","Confident","Sexy","Financially secure", "Supportive","Dresses well","A good listener","Loyal","Successful", "Adventurous","Good job","Religious","Patient", "Extraverted, enthusiastic","Critical, quarrelsome", "Dependable, self-disciplined","Anxious, easily upset", "Open to new experiences","Reserved, quiet","Sympathetic, warm", "Disorganized, careless","Calm, emotionally stable", "Conventional, uncreative","Smells good" ) # beta3 coefficients extracted from Eastwick et al. (2024) publication east_betas_table3 <-c( .02,.03,.04,.00,.02,.02,.07,.07,.02,.06, .04,.02,.04,.02,.04,.01,.03,.01,.03,.05, .05,.05,.13,.01,.07,.08,.03,.07,.05,.09, .02,.04,.03,.07,.01 ) # Storage results_repl <-data.frame( trait = traits_table3, label = labels_table3, beta_eastwick = east_betas_table3, r2m_east = NA_real_, r2c_east = NA_real_, # Interaction (level metric) beta_repl = NA, se_repl = NA, t_repl = NA, p_repl = NA, # Partner trait main effect beta_repl_trait = NA, se_repl_trait = NA, p_repl_trait = NA, # Ideal main effect beta_repl_ideal = NA, se_repl_ideal = NA, p_repl_ideal = NA, converged = NA, stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # ============================================================ # Loop over all 35 traits # ============================================================ for (i in seq_along(traits_table3)) { trait <-traits_table3[i] # Big Five ideals have capital "Ideal_" prefix if (trait %in% c("Ext1","Agr1","Con1","Neu1","Ope1", "Ext2","Agr2","Con2","Neu2","Ope2")) { ideal_v <-paste0("ZIdeal_", trait) } else { ideal_v <-paste0("Zideal_", trait) } partner_v <-paste0("ZP1_", trait) <-scale(dat[[paste0( ifelse(trait %in% c("Ext1","Agr1","Con1","Neu1","Ope1", "Ext2","Agr2","Con2","Neu2","Ope2"), "Ideal_", "ideal_"), trait)]])[,1] dat [[partner_v]] <-scale(dat[[paste0("P1_", trait)]])[,1] # Fit model -random intercept + random slope on partner trait model <-tryCatch({ m <-lmer( as.formula(paste0( "ZP1Eval ~", ideal_v, " + ", partner_v, " + ", ideal_v, ":", partner_v, " + (1 + ", partner_v, " | UserLanguage)" )), data = dat, REML = TRUE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa") ) results_repl[i, "converged"] <-TRUE m }, error = function(e) { message("Random slope failed for ", trait, " -intercept only") results_repl[i, "converged"] <<-FALSE lmer( as.formula(paste0( "ZP1Eval ~", ideal_v, " + ", partner_v, " + ", ideal_v, ":", partner_v, " + (1 | UserLanguage )" )), data = dat, REML = TRUE, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa") ) }) # Extract all three coefficients per model coefs <-summary(model)$coefficients int_term <-paste0(ideal_v, ":", partner_v) r2_tmp <-tryCatch(r.squaredGLMM(model), error = function(e) c(NA_real_, NA_real_)) results_repl[i, "r2m_east"] <-r2_tmp[1] results_repl[i, "r2c_east"] <-r2_tmp[2] # Figure 4 revealed a theoretically meaningful divergence between Model 4 and the Eastwick et al. (2024) replication.
Partner attribute main effects, as presented in Panel 1 were comparatively large and positive in the Eastwick et al.

Eastwick et al. (2024) replication reversed sign in Model 4: Dresses well (.24 to -.06***), Sporty and athletic (.09 to -.05***), Extraverted, enthusiastic (.12 to -.05***), Nice body (.33 → -.03**), and Confident (.15 → -.03**).

H2, which can be derived from Layer 2 implications, receives clearer support when considering partner attribute main effects.

Simultaneously entering all 35 partner attribute ratings alongside demographics produces a stark and consistent compression relative to the Eastwick et al. (2024) trait-bytrait replication, indicating substantial intertrait-confounding or mediation.

The variance decomposition confirms this compression effect: the average fixed variance explained across all 35 trait-by-trait analyses was 'only' about four-and-a-half times smaller than the total variance explained by Model 4.
Further support for H2 is provided by including all ideal preferences main effects in Model 3.
Virtually all ideal attribute ratings were as well substantially attenuated in comparison to theEastwick et al. (2024) sobering picture.
text.formatted: Virtually all ideal attribute ratings were as well substantially attenuated in comparison to the<ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eastwick et al. (2024)</ref> sobering picture.

text.text: Confounding by demographic and individual-difference background characteristics contributes negligibly variance but substantial effect sizes apart from preference-matching predictors, partly supporting H1.
Intertrait confounding severely inflates partner attribute and ideal preference main effects as well as preference-matching interaction coefficients in the trait-by-trait approach.
Multivariate adjustment as provided by Model 4 clearly attenuates all three of them, strongly supporting H2.
Even after this adjustment, preference-matching interactions cluster near zero, with only three of 35 effects reaching significance at the p < .001 threshold, supporting H3.
